articles.title: England v Sri Lanka: first men’s one-day cricket international – live
articles.summary: Over-by-over updates, first ODI from 12.30pm BST Sign up to get The Spin newsletter | And mail Taha England: Ben Duckett, Tom Banton, Joe Root, Harry Brook (c), Jos Buttler (wk), Rehan Ahmed, Will Jacks, Jamie Overton, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Josh Tongue Sri Lanka: Pathum Nissanka, Kamindu Mendis, Kusal Mendis (c, wk), Pavan Rathnayake, Charith Asalanka, Janith Liyanage, Dunith Wellalage, Dushmantha Chameera, Sachindu Colombage, Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka Continue reading...
articles.content:
There’s an international debut for the legspinner Sachindu Colombage. Some ask to come in and bowl at that England middle order. I’m fascinated to see how Rehan Ahmed, carded at six, goes; he’s in because Adil Rashid has an issue with his bowling hand.

England: Ben Duckett, Tom Banton, Joe Root, Harry Brook (c), Jos Buttler (wk), Rehan Ahmed, Will Jacks, Jamie Overton, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Josh Tongue

Sri Lanka: Pathum Nissanka, Kamindu Mendis, Kusal Mendis (c, wk), Pavan Rathnayake, Charith Asalanka, Janith Liyanage, Dunith Wellalage, Dushmantha Chameera, Sachindu Colombage, Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka

Wood is part of Sky’s commentary team for this game, and he’s joined by his former captain Eoin Morgan. They take in the toss … which is won by Harry Brook. England will have a hit.

The big news this morning is that Mark Wood has called it a day at the highest level. Go to his Cricinfo profile and the numbers won’t jump out … but that doesn’t tell his story. You’re better off heading to YouTube to watch that spell at Headingley or the one in St Lucia, bowling at absurd pace. The body, inevitably, suffered. He took 18 wickets when England won the 2019 World Cup and nine at 12 when they won the T20 equivalent in 2022. He won the Ashes at home and, while things didn’t work out for the collective, he thrived in Australia, too. Some career.

Hello, hello, hello and welcome to the last series of the English summer, stretching its way right until the close of September. It’s back to 50-over cricket, the forgotten child, with Sri Lanka hoping that the longer form gives them more of a chance; the T20 series was a miserable affair for the visitors, with defeats by 119 runs, six wickets (47 balls to spare) and eight wickets (62 balls).

After a few lean years in the ODI game, England have won their last two series, away to Sri Lanka at the start of the year and then at home against India. Brendon McCullum has lost the Test job but his white-ball group have had a pretty impressive 2026. It would be quite the splash if Kusal Mendis’ side halt the streak here. We get going in Durham at 12.30pm BST.

articles.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
articles.summary: Ineos said natural gas in the UK is twelve times more expensive than in the US.
articles.content:
Sir Jim said Ineos was being 'forced' to pause production at the three plants

Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices.

The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors.

Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete."

The facilities produce raw materials used to make pharmaceuticals, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction materials and military explosives in the UK and Europe. Gas is a key ingredient in production.

Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site.

But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down.

Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU — where most of its products are exported to — to put in tariff protections against Chinese products.

One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee.

He said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale".

The wholesale price of natural gas — used for heating homes and generating electricity — has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world.

Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents.

Two plants are already shut and a third will stop production in the coming days, the company said.

It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy.

He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Édouard Mendy: ‘Winning Afcon was 10 times better than the Champions League’

articles.content:
After retiring from international football, the former Chelsea keeper reflects on a Senegal career that – according to him – included two African titles

“I had to stay patient and try to have a cool head because everywhere else there was fire,” Édouard Mendy remembers. In the cauldron of the Stade Prince Moulay Abdellah in Rabat, the Senegal goalkeeper was about to face a penalty against the hosts, Morocco, in stoppage time of the Africa Cup of Nations final.

Mendy had just been shown a yellow card after a 17-minute delay where he and most of his teammates had controversially headed to their dressing room in protest at the referee’s decision to penalise El Hadji Malick Diouf after a Morocco corner.

Senegal had also had a goal disallowed minutes earlier, while Mendy’s complaints to the Congolese referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, about having his towel stolen by Ismael Saibari – a misdemeanour for which the Bayern Munich forward later apologised – and lasers being directed in his eyes from the crowd seemed to fall on deaf ears. Now the goalkeeper who won the Champions League with Chelsea in 2021 tried to maintain his focus as Real Madrid’s Brahim Díaz stood over the ball.

“I realised two steps before he shot … usually when a player does a Panenka they slow down for the last step, but I noticed he did it early,” says Mendy, who is widely regarded as one of the best African goalkeepers having played a central role in the most successful period in Senegal’s history. “I know his preferred side is on the right. But when I saw him slow down way before, I just stood up and managed to catch the ball.”

Four minutes into extra time, Pape Gueye’s goal meant Senegal and Mendy crowned African champions for the second time in four years . Or so it seemed. More than seven months after Morocco were awarded a 3-0 victory in March when the Confederation of African Football ruled Senegal had forfeited the final by leaving the pitch , a preliminary hearing for their appeal is finally set to be heard at the court of arbitration for sport in Switzerland next month.

“The only thing we have to remember is that the game went to the end. We went off the pitch but the game restarted,” Mendy said. “For me there is no issue because the final was completed – we were given the trophy and celebrated in our country. That was it. When you speak to me about the Afcon, I just simply tell you that: ‘Yes, we have won it twice.’ That’s nothing against the Moroccan people or anyone else. It’s just how we feel. I’m not a lawyer but it’s just common sense. You can’t change something that has already been decided.”

In the meantime, Mendy has added to his bulging trophy cabinet by winning a second successive Asian Champions League with Al-Ahli, faced World Cup heartache after sustaining a knee injury against Norway and, at the age of 34, announced his international retirement last week. Even a phone call from Senegal’s new manager, Patrick Vieira , could not persuade him to change his mind and potentially add to his 59 caps.

“He [Vieira] is a legend so to have the chance to work with him was really something that came into my mind,” Mendy says. “But at the end of the call I asked for some time to really think about everything. A couple of days later I called him and explained that I wanted to stick to my decision. I started thinking about it after the Afcon and I just came to the conclusion that it was my time to say stop.”

Mendy has high hopes that Senegal’s next generation, which includes Monaco’s Lamine Camara – the midfielder who almost joined Chelsea in the summer – and Aston Villa’s Ibrahim Mbaye can emulate the achievements of his. The Teranga Lions were crowned African champions for the first time in 2022, around eight months after Mendy kept a clean sheet in the 2021 Champions League final. But he says there is no comparison between the two when he looks back now. “[Winning Afcon] was the best moment of my football career: it was 10 times better [than the Champions League]. I can compare now because I’ve also won the Asian Champions League twice.

“To win for your club is something really incredible. But you cannot compare with winning for your country, especially when they have never won anything before. It happens only once in your life so being part of the team that made history was amazing.”

Mendy’s exploits in 2021 led to him being named best goalkeeper at Fifa’s now defunct The Best awards, but he missed out on the Yashin trophy awarded by the organisers of the Ballon d’Or to Gianluigi Donnarumma. Both have been nominated again for this year’s award and Mendy says he is proud to be in the conversation again after what he describes as “my best year since I became a professional” after a season in which no other goalkeeper won as many major honours.

He says: “To be nominated for the Yashin trophy while I play in Saudi Arabia means a lot to me. My journey has not been easy – everything is about working hard and being resilient. When I see goalkeepers in Senegal wearing the No 16 jersey it makes me so proud. It means that at some point I gave them some inspiration and this is very powerful.”

Mendy was born in Normandy, and started his professional career at Cherbourg but found himself unemployed for a year after enduring successive relegations . He was eventually given another chance by Marseille and is now helping to fund a school in his parents’ hometown of Keur Massar that has recently expanded to 200 students. Mendy is also behind a scheme that supports budding entrepreneurs in the country.

“There is so much talent in Senegal and we have a young population that is very dynamic. That’s why it’s important to give them the opportunity to have a better life,” he says. “When my mum sees the school she is so proud and that is the biggest gift anyone can have.”

articles.title: ‘Our job was not to attack’: how do you make a documentary about America’s culture wars?
articles.summary: Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson’s docuseries Bucks County, USA examines the political divide in one town in a revealing and infuriating manner Like many teenage best friends, Evi and Vanessa have a penchant for finishing each other’s sentences. Whether enmeshed on a couch or telling a story, one, a red-headed musical theater nerd with a personality nearly as boisterous as her signature puffy skirts, collides with the other, darker in hair and disposition, their speech bubbling with indecipherable affirmations and giggles. In a heady chorus of “duuude” and “no, you!”, it can be difficult to tell where one girl ends and the other begins. Except, that is, at their respective homes. Evi’s mother, Lela, who like her daughter, espouses views considered left of liberal in the US context, speaks in support of LGBTQ students at local school board meetings and advocates for fact-based history lessons. Vanessa’s father, Paul Martino, is a right-leaning venture capitalist who likes to brag about installing school board members by spending $500,000 on local campaigns, an effort triggered by what he saw as unjustified school closures in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic. articles.content:
Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson’s docuseries Bucks County, USA examines the political divide in one town in a revealing and infuriating manner

L ike many teenage best friends, Evi and Vanessa have a penchant for finishing each other’s sentences. Whether enmeshed on a couch or telling a story, one, a red-headed musical theater nerd with a personality nearly as boisterous as her signature puffy skirts, collides with the other, darker in hair and disposition, their speech bubbling with indecipherable affirmations and giggles. In a heady chorus of “duuude” and “no, you!”, it can be difficult to tell where one girl ends and the other begins.

Except, that is, at their respective homes. Evi’s mother, Lela, who like her daughter, espouses views considered left of liberal in the US context, speaks in support of LGBTQ students at local school board meetings and advocates for fact-based history lessons. Vanessa’s father, Paul Martino, is a right-leaning venture capitalist who likes to brag about installing school board members by spending $500,000 on local campaigns, an effort triggered by what he saw as unjustified school closures in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic.

That their parents do not see eye to eye is an understatement; both are actively involved – on social media, on Zoom and in the meeting room – in lobbying their local school district board, and frequently call out the other by name. Like many towns across the US, the girls’ home in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, an affluent district north of Philadelphia, has been roiled by the political and cultural currents triggered by upheaval of Covid-19. Seemingly overnight, concerns that simmered in various social media forums and side chats – the legality of masking, critical race theory, DEI, slavery, election conspiracy theories and viral fixations over transgender students and bathrooms – concentrated in perhaps the one unifying place in town: the school, and in particular its governing board, whose public meetings frequently ended in ugly shouting matches. Evi and Vanessa may open each episode of Bucks County, USA, a new five-part PBS docuseries embedded in one emblematically polarized town, in unison, but the adults, it seems, could not stop fighting.

The series, directed by Robert May and Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson, of Rain Man glory, and filmed over four highly contentious years, plays out a roving gallery of 2020s US politics in miniature – a “microcosm for communities around the country”, said May, where concern for one’s children morphs and mutates into hardline stances. Good intentions and, at times, bad information collide with pride in familiar, if fascinating and infuriating, stalemates. “We’re not trying to be political, to point fingers about this and that,” Levinson said of the dispassionate series, which gives many town-members free range to express their views. “We’re looking into what happened in an area that was almost idyllic – what threw us that far out of whack?”

By the time the film-makers arrived in town in late 2021, inspired by a two-part episode from the New York Times’ The Daily podcast, the Central Bucks school board was already riven with conflict. Pushback to the district’s mask policy and Covid closures, along with Martino’s money via a Pac, fueled previously inconceivable attack ads and fake fliers. A new conservative majority on the board had turned their attention to certain books, which were either “grooming” children or LGBTQ-positive, depending on who was doing the talking. And talk people did, from parents to students to former teachers, from board members with pride bumper stickers on their cars to a parent speaker affiliated with Moms for Liberty, the Florida-based rightwing group that built an outsized influence on school boards across the country primarily via book ban campaigns .

“We wanted to talk to people from both sides that really had a point of view,” May explained, letting curiosity be their guide to a true cross-section of the town’s ideological landscape. Interviews often began with personal questions and with promises to not interrupt, which were greeted warmly, particularly by conservative townspeople more skittish about a film crew. “It’s a rarity for someone to be able to speak for 30 seconds without someone firing back a counterpoint, and neither one of them then are listening to one another,” said May. “Our job was not to attack the person that’s sharing their opinion, but allowing them to share their opinion, to allow multiple sides to share an opinion and let the audience decide.

“We know that there will be critics that will see this series, looking at someone that they don’t like, and they will say, ‘well, they were lying, and we should have told them that or called them out on it,’” he added when I noted the potential for false equivalencies. “And of course, if you have that point of view about it, you missed the whole point of the series.”

Or Martino, who argues “equity is not a fundamentally American principle”, and a Black parent who recognizes that “for someone to say they don’t want diversity, equity and inclusion … then to me, you’re saying you don’t want my family here.”

There isn’t, really, though May and Levinson remain hopeful through the effort of trying. “We didn’t necessarily witness folks that changed their political persuasion or changed their political view, but we did witness people that agreed to figure out how to talk to one another and come together,” said May, particularly in a final series roundtable, after the first two episodes’ 2025 Sundance premiere, where both conversation and tensions flare. “You see it throughout the series – there’s an effort,” said May. “It doesn’t all get wrapped up in a bow by any means. articles.title: Henry Pollock saga ends after player signs ‘multi-year’ deal to stay at Northampton
articles.summary: ‘I’m happy. It’s an exciting place to be right now’ Prem champions have moved to tie down huge asset England back row Henry Pollock has signed a bumper new contract with Northampton. The 21-year-old has agreed a “multi-year” deal, the Prem champions announced on Tuesday morning. “I’m massively happy to re-sign with Saints, my boyhood club,” Pollock said. “It’s an exciting place to be right now. We’re in a great spot as a team, but it feels like there’s still so much more growth in us.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
England back row Henry Pollock has signed a bumper new contract with Northampton . The 21-year-old has agreed a “multi-year” deal, the Prem champions announced on Tuesday morning.

“I’m massively happy to re-sign with Saints, my boyhood club,” Pollock said. “It’s an exciting place to be right now. We’re in a great spot as a team, but it feels like there’s still so much more growth in us.”

Pollock has had a rapid rise to the top of the sport and recently became the first rugby player to be represented by Barry and Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom Talent Agency. And, famous for promoting boxing, darts and snooker, the Hearns have got straight to work, negotiating Pollock a contract widely reported to be in excess of £400,000 per year.

Pollock, who has played 13 times for England and won five British and Irish Lions caps, added: “I’m still young, and we’ve got a young squad with a brilliant group of lads. Some of my best mates are here, and every day everyone pushes each other to improve and be the best players and team we can be. For where I am in my career, this is exactly where I want to be. I feel like we’re only just getting started. We won the Prem last season and we want to go again.

“Winning the Champions Cup is another huge ambition for us. We came so close a couple of years ago, and achieving that together would be incredibly special. I just want to enjoy every moment of this journey. I’m playing for my boyhood club, surrounded by great people, and that’s something I never take for granted. The connections within this group are what make it such a special place.”

Northampton’s director of rugby Phil Dowson believes it is important for the club to tie down a player who is transcending the sport. He said: “We’re delighted that Henry has committed his future to Saints. Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he’s a young man of outstanding character.

“Keeping someone with both his talent and mindset is hugely important for the club. What’s most exciting is that there’s still so much more to come from him. Henry is incredibly ambitious and constantly looking for ways to improve.

“He’s become an important figure not just for Saints, but for the wider game. He inspires young supporters, brings excitement to rugby, and understands that everything off the pitch is built on performing consistently on it. We’re excited to see what he can achieve over the coming years.”

articles.content:
With added coverage comes added scrutiny and there is a feeling that the league was too lenient when punishing chants about the late Portugal forward

T he good thing about Cristiano Ronaldo playing in your league is that he is one of the most famous footballers ever and when he scores a great goal or reaches 1,000 (just 21 to go), many people watch. The bad thing about Cristiano Ronaldo playing in your league is that when something negative happens and he is involved, just as many people will watch and listen. Global attention is something that the big European leagues have had for years but it is something the Saudi Pro League, which has spent billions in search of achieving a similar stature, needs to get used to.

On Sunday 13 September, Ronaldo wrote to his 680 million Instagram followers to discuss the events of Saturday evening. That was when Al-Taawoun supporters were coming to terms with a 6-0 home thrashing by Al-Hilal, whose £150m-plus forward line, Ollie Watkins and Gabriel Martinelli , got five between them. Fair to say that some handled it better than others as what followed was in the worst possible taste.

At the end, what seemed to be a small number of fans saw Al-Hilal’s Rúben Neves in the centre circle and started chanting the name of his former Portugal and Wolves teammate Diogo Jota, who tragically died in a car accident in July 2025. Neves, who has a tattoo of the Liverpool star, was visibly upset and made a gesture which clearly said to those supporters that “God is watching you”. He also said to Saudi reporters after the game: “I hope they don’t go to pray afterwards.”

Ronaldo then weighed in . “The league must take ⁠action and punish this kind of fan behaviour,” he wrote. “This is no longer football, and there have to be limits. People who behave ‌like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again.” Al-Hilal made an official complaint. This was a big story.

Ayman al-Hotami, one of Al-Hilal’s best-known fans, says: “I found the chants hard to believe but those responsible were few in number and very young. Al-Hilal’s fanbase completely condemn the chants and demanded an apology regarding the actions of individuals in their stands. We appreciate the club’s response in condemning this isolated incident, which represents neither the club nor our society.”

Away from home in small stadiums with low attendances, often the case when the big teams play outside Jeddah and Riyadh, the chants of a few can carry far. More than once, Ronaldo has heard the name of a certain Argentinian star coming his way and reacted badly . This, though, was on a completely different level.

The well-known Saudi broadcaster Waleed al-Faraj says: “To shout ‘Messi’ at Ronaldo is acceptable within the context of the rivalry between them, but to chant the name of his deceased teammate Jota at Neves is an inappropriate act. How can you play on people’s grief like this? You should have some humanity.”

The Saudi legend Sami al-Jaber, who played at four World Cups and had a short spell in England with Wolves, sent a message to Neves: “Rúben, your presence in Saudi football means a great deal to us. As Saudis, we take pride in our values of respect and hospitality … they transcend any sporting rivalry. This behaviour does not reflect those values. I hope you know how warmly you are regarded here, and how much you belong.”

Ronaldo’s call for action was met four days later. “The Saudi Arabian Football Federation (Saff) and the Saudi Pro League (SPL) condemn the unacceptable conduct by some supporters in attendance,” a statement said, adding that the chants were inconsistent with the values of Saudi football and sportsmanship in general. Al-Taawoun have been handed a ban of around £20,000 and ordered to play two matches behind closed doors . An earlier statement said that “exploiting personal tragedies for the purpose of abuse or provocation is unacceptable behaviour that has no place in Saudi football”.

Some felt that more could have been made of an opportunity to send a message to the rest of the league, one of zero tolerance and harsh punishments for those individuals responsible. Nobody would have complained – Al Taawoun had condemned what happened and said it was “not representative of their supporters”. Here was a clearcut case of fans behaving badly as you are going to get.

European football has worked hard to try and stamp out offensive chants. “Stadiums in places such as Portugal and England are nowadays heavily controlled spaces,” says Simon Chadwick, professor of Afro-Eurasian Sport at Emlyon Business School in Paris. “Hence, when someone like Ronaldo encounters [verbal abuse] he will inevitably respond, thereby attracting attention from the media and others. Saudi Arabian fans need to get used to such a reaction fast.” It is not just the international media that get involved. “Organisations such as the AFC and Fifa may even implement codes of conduct and penalties for situations like the Jota episode,” Chadwick says. “In other words, if Saudi fans and/or the Pro League can’t regulate or control the situation, then someone else will.”

With the Asian Cup coming to the country in January for the first time – and preparation for the 2034 World Cup on the way – Saudi Arabia will be hoping that such action will not be necessary.

articles.title: ‘Hardships never last’: Jenn Lichter’s path from Colombian orphanage to ultrarunning records
articles.summary: Jenn Lichter’s childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summer On 27 June, Jenn Lichter lined up for her first 100-mile race, the Western States 100. The oldest and most prestigious 100-miler in the world, Western States attracts a highly competitive field from around the globe – the athletes run across the Sierra Nevada from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California. Despite 18,000ft of climbing and daytime temperatures often flirting with triple digits, Lichter went in confident. “I wanted to win, there was no secret to that,” she says. “That’s just who I am.” The race remained close for the first half, until the 30-year-old made a move on the climb to Devil’s Thumb. The gap grew and at the final aid station, Lichter had a sizable lead over the athlete in second place. A mile from the finish, Nick Cornell, Lichter’s fiance, told her she was just ahead of the course record. “That was the first I had heard about it,” Lichter says. “He knew my competitive side would jump at the challenge.” Continue reading...

The race remained close for the first half, until the 30-year-old made a move on the climb to Devil’s Thumb. The gap grew and at the final aid station, Lichter had a sizable lead over the athlete in second place. A mile from the finish, Nick Cornell, Lichter’s fiance, told her she was just ahead of the course record. “That was the first I had heard about it,” Lichter says. “He knew my competitive side would jump at the challenge.”

Lichter sprinted the final mile down the streets of Auburn and on to the Placer High track, breaking the tape in 15 hours 28 minutes 5 seconds, 88 seconds faster than Courtney Dauwalter’s previous course record. Before 2026, only one woman had come within 50 minutes of Dauwalter’s time, making the record seem nearly unbreakable to most fans. Two months later, Lichter is only just putting that moment into perspective.

“It took a while to process,” Lichter says. “It’s only hitting as I’m wrapping up the season and have the time to look back and realize what I did. It’s like summiting one of the most beautiful peaks in the world and at first you can’t fully understand what you’re seeing.”

Lichter’s road to that record-shattering win was far from traditional. She was born in Bogotá, Colombia, and at two years old she was picked up by childcare services and placed in an orphanage, along with her older brother and younger sister. Her father had been shot and killed while involved with drug cartels and her mother struggled with addiction, leaving the children to fend for themselves on the streets.

“Life in the orphanage was very regimented,” Lichter says. “Breakfast, lunch, dinner, and recess were always at the same time, but ignorance is bliss. When you’re a kid, you don’t know better.” Lichter’s mom would visit on the weekends, while trying to get back on her feet. When Lichter was seven, she and her siblings, Harold and Kim, were moved to an orphanage that worked to get them adopted together.

“Despite the circumstances, we were happy and a big reason for that is we had each other,” she says. “That kept our mental state intact and made the whole experience less frightening. From birth, we’ve felt attached at the hip. Like twins, we can feel each other’s emotions. Our souls are intertwined.”

Through those years, Lichter also learned how to rely on herself to get through challenges. “If shit ever hits the fan, I just pick myself up and dust myself off and continue on,” she says. “Life can be hard but it doesn’t mean you have to succumb to it. Hardships never last for ever.”

When she was nine, Lichter and her siblings were adopted by a family in La Crosse, Wisconsin, on the banks of the Mississippi. She only knew a handful of English words – hello and goodbye, water, a few colors – so her adopted parents hired a bilingual nanny to help translate, carried a dictionary everywhere they went and covered the house in sticky notes with Spanish words and their English equivalent together, to help the kids learn the new language.

The biggest culture shock for Lichter was the freedom she suddenly had. “I remember thinking, what do you mean we can have a snack whenever we want? Go outside whenever we want? Have a toy that’s not communal? Have seconds at dinner? The little, simple things that most people take for granted were everything to us.”

Her new life was much more freeing than her time in the orphanage – going out to restaurants, road trips, and meeting new friends – but it came with challenges. “The language was hard at first, but I trusted that the longer I was in it, the better I would get,” Lichter says. “After a year I was fluent, happy and felt secure.”

In elementary school Lichter played basketball and enjoyed it, but in middle school she stopped growing and felt out of place. Her mom suggested cross-country running, which Lichter had never heard of. “I tried it out and thought it was the most uncomfortable thing in the world,” she says, “but I also had a sense that I could keep going.”

Lichter stuck it out for a season, mostly out of curiosity. She found success and was recruited by the high school team, but the sport soon turned dark for her. “I liked the competition,” Lichter says, “but truly I like it because it was just something I could control. It’s just you, your body and your thoughts. That’s where the obsession started.”

Running brought up the trauma around leaving Colombia that Lichter had repressed for years. She wrestled with the feeling of abandonment and used running as an outlet, driven by a search for control. At 12, Lichter was diagnosed with anorexia and for the next three years was in and out of treatment centers, working through the emotions of leaving her birth mother and loving her adopted mother.

As a senior in high school, Lichter started winning races, sometimes by minutes. She received offers from a number of Division III and Division II schools, but instead opted for a walk-on scholarship from University of Toledo, her only Division I offer. “I felt like working for my spot would bring out the best in me,” Lichter says. “I had a fantastic freshman year, then dealt with RED-S [ relative energy deficiency in sport ] the rest of college. After that, I didn’t think running was meant to be in my life.”

After graduating, Lichter packed up her car and roadtripped west with her mother, with plans to land in Portland, Oregon. Along the way they visited Montana’s Glacier national park and Lichter immediately fell in love. After the trip, Lichter stayed in Portland just 10 days before packing up again and driving back to Montana. “I had this moment when I realized I was a grown adult and I could do what I want,” she says, “so I drove back to Kalispell and the rest is history.”

She started working as a hiking guide, living out of her tent for much of the summer. “I was 23 and felt so alive,” Lichter says. “I thought I’d hit the apex of my life, found my dream job.”

That’s where Lichter met Cornell, who also worked as a guide. On their days off, they would go on trail runs together, and the joy of running slowly came back to Lichter. In the fall of 2021, Cornell suggested they race The Rut 50k in Big Sky, Montana.

“I didn’t realize I still had the competitive spirit in me until we were driving to the race and I told Nick I wanted to win,” says Lichter, who went on to run the third fastest time in course history. After the race, The North Face offered Lichter her first professional trail running contract, and she jumped at the opportunity.

Lichter recommitted to running, but planned to do it differently this time around. “In middle school and high school and college I had snippets of potential, but kept getting in my own way,” she says Licht. “Now I’m focused on taking care of myself first … actually taking easy runs easy, and not running myself into the ground. My sense of control is a lot different than it used to be.”

That refreshed mentality has paid dividends. Lichter has won some of the most competitive 50k races around the United States – The Rut twice more, Broken Arrow Skyrace twice, Speedgoat and Gorge Waterfalls. Last year she decided to bump up in distance and told her team manager that her goal was to win Western States. To do that, she first had to qualify.

Lichter lined up for the Black Canyon 100k in February, surrounded by a stacked field all wanting to earn a golden ticket to Western States. She won by mere seconds. After four more months of training, Lichter did the unthinkable, breaking Dauwalter’s record at the country’s most competitive 100-mile race.

With months to reflect, Lichter says very little has changed after stunning the trail running world. “I feel more confident, but truthfully, my life is still the same,” she says. “I just keep putting in the work and being willing to take shots at new things. With my two feet on the ground, I have a sense of safety and control I used to not have, which gives me the confidence to try just about anything.”

articles.content:
The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism

T here is a single minute in Buy the Dip, Nimesh Patel’s new Netflix comedy special, in which the comedian nimbly and hilariously goes from describing his wife in labour with their first child to complaining about a Rolex sporting doctor wearing “insurance payments on his wrist” to Luigi Mangione . “He killed one guy, allegedly,” Patel quips, arguing that the terrorism-related charge Mangione got stuck with (which a judge dismissed ) was offensive to real terrorists.

The hilarious bit is impressive for how much Patel packs into a single minute and how much it all speaks to the comedian’s own experience, expertise and worldview.

Patel, who hails from New Jersey, was once a pre-med finance graduate from New York University. He entertained going into healthcare before joining the ranks of finance bros. He abandoned all of that when he found a path in comedy alongside the likes of Hasan Minhaj and Rami Malek , a generation of brown guys who came of age in the shadow of 9/11 and have had to grow up being associated with Al-Qaida by the most racist swaths of American society. Patel is maybe the only one of them who could land that punchline about Mangione, which exists in the exact same intersection as him: of healthcare, finance and charges of terrorism that don’t stick.

“It wasn’t by design that I was going to condense all that into that bit,” Patel says, humbly, on a Zoom call from his home in Brooklyn, New York. “It just so happened that that’s where my brain goes.”

The words “it just so happened” gets at Patel’s magic trick as a comedian. In Buy the Dip, and across a lot of his comedy found online , Patel maintains the most laidback, effortless and unbothered vibe. He’s the kind of stand-up who makes it genuinely seem as though he’s floating along and the jokes just so happen to make their way to him.

Patel understands that passive air to be both a feature and a bug. Throughout our conversation he looks back at moments in his life and career, at times with regret, where he “didn’t deal well with adversity” (he gave up on pre-med after getting a C in one class) or he let fate decide his life choices for him. On the latter front, for instance, Patel lost his job in finance in 2016, at the same time that Chris Rock discovered him at the Comedy Cellar in New York, where he had been performing and honing his craft for years.

“It was a very star-aligning kind of a moment,” says Patel, looking back at how the decision to commit full-time to comedy was made for him. Rock tapped the newly unemployed Patel to write for his hosting duties at the 2016 Oscars , which led to, among other things, Patel becoming the first Indian American to join the writer’s room at SNL, where he lasted a single season that nabbed him an Emmy nomination .

“I’ll happily admit that I was not good at those jobs,” he adds. “I was still finding and having to cultivate my own voice. I have my own way of delivering my jokes in my worldview. To then recalibrate that and figure out how someone else would say it is actually a pretty difficult thing. Some of those joke writers are the best joke writers on the planet, but I’m a very good stand-up.”

Through our conversation, Patel’s brain regularly goes to finance, whether he’s crunching the numbers on ticket sales growth at his shows (“I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok”) or casually dropping a reference to Apple and Nvidia’s stock growth while calculating what he sacrificed (a $125,000 payday) when backing out of the Saudi Arabia-sponsored Riyadh comedy festival last year. “I’ve said and I stated, if it was more money, I definitely would have gone,” says Patel, being bluntly honest about the accounting that would trump his moral discomfort with a festival sponsored by the Saudi Arabian government.

Even the title to his special, Buy the Dip, is a finance phrase for buying stock while it’s low, which Patel wields playfully. On the one hand, it’s a reference to Donald Trump’s corruption, a big talking point in the special. Over the past year, the president’s tariffs wreaked havoc on the stock market. In April 2025, Trump posted advice to followers on his social media platform Truth Social to buy stock, hours before he announced a pause on tariffs that saw stocks bounce back. “You can’t say ‘buy the dip’ after causing the dip,” says Patel, sounding exasperated. “It seems illegal.”

“I have a kid,” says Patel. “I’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the face. ‘Buy the dip’ is such an optimistic phrase. It says things will get better. You just gotta believe. Sometimes things get bad but if you, if your thesis remains the same, if you have conviction, you will be rewarded.”

Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates parenting while prodding at the broken healthcare system, Maga and anti-immigrant sentiments, all while maintaining that hopeful and yet still unbothered vibe I’ve seen in his social media clips.

Patel first landed on my radar because TikTok’s algorithms served me a viral crowd-work clip , recorded at New York’s Comedy Cellar in 2018, when the comic was interacting with an Israeli musician who said he makes “progressive rock”. In one of those moments where a joke just seemed to materialize on the spot, Patel asked what Israeli progressive rock would sound like, before miming guitar play and singing, “Free Palestine”. The room erupted. Even Patel, in that moment, was visibly astonished at how he came up with that.

“That clip has had a long shelf life,” says Patel, sharing regret that the joke has only grown more relevant in the years since and that he wasn’t more prepared to go in-depth at the time. In that 2018 interaction, Patel claims ignorance on Israel’s war on Gaza , and shrinks from taking a stand on the issue. “I wish, at that time, I had more of a knowledge base about the conflict to really dig in on it.”

“It should be obvious,” adds Patel, speaking to his position on the matter over the years since. “It should be obvious what my position is because the instant you see the genocide in Gaza, as a brown person, [you know] that is the position of the oppressed.”

Patel, whose wife is Jewish, is much more pointed on the issue in Buy the Dip. He has a bit where he speaks out against making false equivalencies between Judaism and the Israeli regime. But then he can’t resist trolling with a punchline knowingly predicated on that very same false equivalency. “When it hits,” says Patel, “it hits really hard.”

I push back on the idea that Patel’s position on Israel and Palestine, as a brown person, should be obvious, because there are so many brown people who do support Israel’s actions. Patel gets that. He points to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, as an example. Modi, who is accused by many of stoking violent Islamophobia with his Hindu nationalist rhetoric, is a staunch ally to Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu. Though Patel himself is wary of prescribing Islamophobia as the reason behind their alliance. “It is very interesting and confusing partnership on the surface of it. If it’s based in Islamophobia, that seems very superficial.”

“I find it funny that religious people really forget their religion when they start talking about other people’s religions,” says Patel, whose dives into his upbringing within a devout Hindu family in his material. “It’s like the tenet of the Gita to love everybody and treat everybody equally. The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly.”

Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates the ideological rifts between himself and other south Asians. It’s his burden, as an Indian American, as a Patel even, to put some distance between his demographic at large and those whose views or prejudices he doesn’t share. Kash Patel , the FBI director whom the comic refers to as Trump’s brand of DEI (“dick-eating Indian”), is a prime target.

Patel – Nimesh, that is – is also compelled to clock and respond to a rise in anti-Indian sentiment, which he tells me he’s witnessed in videos and online commentary coming from Canada and the US. The situation reared its head just over a week ago when Bo French , the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, posted a viral photo on X of students celebrating the University of Texas’s college football win against Ohio State University. A number of the joyful students in the photo appeared to be of south Asian descent. French, in that post and a subsequent post, decried that foreigners were displacing Americans. On Saturday, after my conversation with Patel, the US Department of Education’s X account seemed to piggyback on French’s sentiments, posting a photo of the crowd at a University of Texas game with the slogans “make college football great again” and “make education great again”.

“Most of those students are probably Indian American,” says Patel. “Those kids likely represent some of the best students in Texas. And they are Americans. They’re rooting football on. They’re drinking beers. What could be more American than that?”

Patel then plays devil’s advocate, speaking directly to the folks who are mad at the sight of Indians, whose anti-immigrant fury is stoked by partisan politics without self-reflection.

“The H-1B program in America was signed into law by [George] Bush, the first one,” says Patel, demanding they address the root cause instead of the symptom. “Corporatists taking over the country wanted cheaper labor that was beholden to the visa. These companies hire people who effectively have a gun to their heads, because if they don’t work, they can just be shipped back.

“I don’t agree with not letting people in at all. Every place is richer and better because of immigrants and what they bring to the countries that they go to. But if you have a problem with immigrants –and you shouldn’t have problems with immigrants – you should be addressing the people on both sides that foster that situation in the first place.”

Patel than takes a step back, turns the lens back on himself and his wider audience, and situates the relationship between the two in this conversation about what it means to be American.

“[Buy the Dip] is probably the most Indian special I’ve put out. It’s Indian in that everything is rooted in an Indian POV. But it’s also deeply American, and I think very universal. I hope people see the optimism in it and take something special away for themselves.”

On the one hand, it’s a reference to Donald Trump’s corruption, a big talking point in the special. Over the past year, the president’s tariffs wreaked havoc on the stock market. In April 2025, Trump posted advice to followers on his social media platform Truth Social to buy stock, hours before he announced a pause on tariffs that saw stocks bounce back. “You can’t say ‘buy the dip’ after causing the dip,” says Patel, sounding exasperated. “It seems illegal.”

“I have a kid,” says Patel. “I’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the face. ‘Buy the dip’ is such an optimistic phrase. It says things will get better. You just gotta believe. Sometimes things get bad but if you, if your thesis remains the same, if you have conviction, you will be rewarded.”

Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates parenting while prodding at the broken healthcare system, Maga and anti-immigrant sentiments, all while maintaining that hopeful and yet still unbothered vibe I’ve seen in his social media clips.

Patel first landed on my radar because TikTok’s algorithms served me a viral crowd-work clip , recorded at New York’s Comedy Cellar in 2018, when the comic was interacting with an Israeli musician who said he makes “progressive rock”. In one of those moments where a joke just seemed to materialize on the spot, Patel asked what Israeli progressive rock would sound like, before miming guitar play and singing, “Free Palestine”. The room erupted. Even Patel, in that moment, was visibly astonished at how he came up with that.

“That clip has had a long shelf life,” says Patel, sharing regret that the joke has only grown more relevant in the years since and that he wasn’t more prepared to go in-depth at the time. In that 2018 interaction, Patel claims ignorance on Israel’s war on Gaza , and shrinks from taking a stand on the issue. “I wish, at that time, I had more of a knowledge base about the conflict to really dig in on it.”

“It should be obvious,” adds Patel, speaking to his position on the matter over the years since. “It should be obvious what my position is because the instant you see the genocide in Gaza, as a brown person, [you know] that is the position of the oppressed.”

Patel, whose wife is Jewish, is much more pointed on the issue in Buy the Dip. He has a bit where he speaks out against making false equivalencies between Judaism and the Israeli regime. But then he can’t resist trolling with a punchline knowingly predicated on that very same false equivalency. “When it hits,” says Patel, “it hits really hard.”

I push back on the idea that Patel’s position on Israel and Palestine, as a brown person, should be obvious, because there are so many brown people who do support Israel’s actions. Patel gets that. He points to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, as an example. Modi, who is accused by many of stoking violent Islamophobia with his Hindu nationalist rhetoric, is a staunch ally to Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu. Though Patel himself is wary of prescribing Islamophobia as the reason behind their alliance. “It is very interesting and confusing partnership on the surface of it. If it’s based in Islamophobia, that seems very superficial.”

“I find it funny that religious people really forget their religion when they start talking about other people’s religions,” says Patel, whose dives into his upbringing within a devout Hindu family in his material. “It’s like the tenet of the Gita to love everybody and treat everybody equally. The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly.”

Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates the ideological rifts between himself and other south Asians. It’s his burden, as an Indian American, as a Patel even, to put some distance between his demographic at large and those whose views or prejudices he doesn’t share. Kash Patel , the FBI director whom the comic refers to as Trump’s brand of DEI (“dick-eating Indian”), is a prime target.

Patel – Nimesh, that is – is also compelled to clock and respond to a rise in anti-Indian sentiment, which he tells me he’s witnessed in videos and online commentary coming from Canada and the US. The situation reared its head just over a week ago when Bo French , the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, posted a viral photo on X of students celebrating the University of Texas’s college football win against Ohio State University. A number of the joyful students in the photo appeared to be of south Asian descent. French, in that post and a subsequent post, decried that foreigners were displacing Americans. On Saturday, after my conversation with Patel, the US Department of Education’s X account seemed to piggyback on French’s sentiments, posting a photo of the crowd at a University of Texas game with the slogans “make college football great again” and “make education great again”.

“Most of those students are probably Indian American,” says Patel. “Those kids likely represent some of the best students in Texas. And they are Americans. They’re rooting football on. They’re drinking beers. What could be more American than that?”
Patel then plays devil’s advocate, speaking directly to the folks who are mad at the sight of Indians, whose anti-immigrant fury is stoked by partisan politics without self-reflection.

“The H-1B program in America was signed into law by [George] Bush, the first one,” says Patel, demanding they address the root cause instead of the symptom. “Corporatists taking over the country wanted cheaper labor that was beholden to the visa. These companies hire people who effectively have a gun to their heads, because if they don’t work, they can just be shipped back.

“I don’t agree with not letting people in at all. Every place is richer and better because of immigrants and what they bring to the countries that they go to. But if you have a problem with immigrants –and you shouldn’t have problems with immigrants – you should be addressing the people on both sides that foster that situation in the first place.”
Patel than takes a step back, turns the lens back on himself and his wider audience, and situates the relationship between the two in this conversation about what it means to be American.

“[Buy the Dip] is probably the most Indian special I’ve put out. It’s Indian in that everything is rooted in an Indian POV. But it’s also deeply American, and I think very universal. I hope people see the optimism in it and take something special away for themselves.”

articles.title: Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to evade Taliban wins Asian Games silver
articles.summary: Fariba Hashimi fled after Taliban returned to power ‘This medal can show resilience from Afghan women’ An Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday, hoping it inspires other women in a country where Taliban authorities have sharply curtailed their freedoms. Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph “something special”. Continue reading...
articles.content:
An Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday, hoping it inspires other women in a country where Taliban authorities have sharply curtailed their freedoms.

Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph “something special”.

“I can’t explain my feelings now,” said the 23-year-old, before reflecting on how she was attacked with stones and trained disguised as a man when she started out in the sport as a teenager along with sister Yulduz, who is also now a pro cyclist. “I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I’m really happy that I have fought against that,” she said. “I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.”

The Taliban authorities returned to power in 2021 and have since imposed a series of rules limiting women’s access to education and public life, including sport.

“They took away our freedom, they took away everything from us,” said Hashimi, who hails from the Faryab province in northern Afghanistan and left the country after the Taliban authorities took over. “This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I’m really happy. I’m not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me.”

After fleeing Afghanistan with the help of Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto, Hashimi relocated to Italy, where she now lives and trains. She and her sister competed at the Paris Olympics two years ago, and the 2028 Los Angeles Games are now looming into view. “I never want to give up and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles,” she said.

Hashimi reserved a special thanks for the Japanese team for playing a part in her silver medal. “I’m here without a mechanic, without any preparation. We brought one guy with us from the national federation, and he just drove the car,” she said. “We were fixing the bike ourselves. I was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself. Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike.”

articles.content:
For the first time in 14 years, Millwall and West Ham faced each other in their 100th meeting. Documentary photographer Adam Isfendiyar was at the Den to record the fans’ matchday experience

When Millwall hosted West Ham at the Den on Saturday, it was the 100th competitive meeting between the clubs, and the first in 14 years.

The pair are separated and connected by the Thames. They were formed around the heavy industries of east London’s docklands in the late 19th century and were geographically much closer then – Millwall on the Isle of Dogs and Thames Ironworks, from which West Ham emerged, around Canning Town. Before Millwall relocated south of the Thames to New Cross in 1910, both were north of the river and only a little over two miles apart.

Now the Lions, Millwall were known as the Dockers during their formative years. West Ham’s nickname, the Irons, refers to their origins among workers at the Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company. Dock work was precarious and physically demanding. Men could turn up each morning with no guarantee of being chosen for work, and competition for a day’s labour could be fierce. That world fostered ideas of toughness, loyalty and hard work which still form part of how both clubs understand and present themselves.

With histories stretching back so far, it can be difficult to separate fact from folklore. One enduring story places the origins of the rivalry in the General Strike of 1926, when West Ham dock workers supposedly supported the strike while those at Millwall did not. Historians David Sullivan and Brian Belton dispute that version. Belton says the strike was solid in the Millwall docks, while only a handful of workers broke ranks around Canning Town. Yet the story has survived for a century and become part of the mythology surrounding the fixture.

The clubs’ histories first crossed in the 1890s, when Millwall Athletic played Thames Ironworks. Belton cautions against treating Thames simply as an earlier West Ham as the company team was dissolved before the new club was formed in 1900. Sullivan and Belton both question the idea of an ancient Dockers Derby. Much of the hostility associated with the fixture today developed later, particularly during the 1970s. There was serious disorder at Harry Cripps’s testimonial in 1972, despite Cripps being well-loved at both clubs, and in 1976 a Millwall supporter died after falling from a train, with some believing West Ham supporters were involved. When the clubs met competitively again in 1978 after a long absence, violence accompanied the fixture.

Mounted police keep fans at bay outside the Den and move across the car park; a Millwall fan shouts at the West Ham team bus as it arrives at the ground; a West Ham fan gesticulates towards Millwall supporters across a barrier blockaded by police.

It is perhaps more than coincidence that the rivalry intensified during the same period in which the industrial world from which both clubs had emerged was disappearing. London’s docks were closing, traditional industries were shedding tens of thousands of jobs and many surrounding communities were experiencing unemployment and economic decline. It would be too simplistic to draw a direct line between industrial decline and football hooliganism, but the two occurred concurrently. Football offered a place in which territory, masculinity, belonging and local pride could still be asserted at a time when some of the institutions that had previously provided those identities were disappearing.

Through the 1980s, 90s and early 2000s, the reputation of the rivalry was reinforced by occasional but memorable flashpoints. The most notorious came at Upton Park in 2009, when a League Cup tie was overshadowed by fighting outside the stadium, a stabbing and pitch invasions. Their two Championship meetings in 2011-12 passed without anything approaching the disorder of 2009, and after that they did not meet competitively again until this season.

Both clubs carry reputations for violence, reinforced by films such as ID and Green Street, and the Dockers Derby amplifies that mythology further. Despite predictable heated posts and banter on social media, there was a general feeling before Saturday that the day would pass without serious trouble, which it mostly did.

There is suspicion towards journalists, including photographers, among both fanbases, and people on both sides warned me to be careful. I had a few choice words thrown at me during the day, but they came from a minority. What was far more visible was the strength of community around the clubs and the friendliness and warmth of the majority of supporters I spoke to and photographed.

West Ham fans making their way to the ground, at the fan zone and inside the Den.

The game was broadcast live on ITV. Kick-off was moved to 12.30pm, limiting the time available for drinking beforehand, and an extensive police operation involving about 400 officers was put in place. West Ham received just 1,774 tickets in a crowd of about 20,000 and most of their supporters avoided wearing club colours. They were instructed to travel via London Bridge to South Bermondsey, from where they were escorted to the away end.

West Ham arrived at the Den top of the table and having recently beaten Wrexham 6-0 , but Millwall, despite dealing with a number of injuries, dominated much of the first half and went into the interval two goals ahead. West Ham found their way back into the game and equalised with 10 minutes remaining. Each goal produced an explosive reaction from the stands, but the equaliser was the only point when the crowd appeared in danger of spilling over, with additional police support called in. In the 89th minute, as Kyrell Lisbie broke through on goal, Mohamadou Kanté pulled him down, earning a straight red card and possibly denying Millwall a winner. It finished 2-2 , a result both clubs could find reasons to be disappointed and satisfied with.

The Lions dominated the first half and the home side went in at the break two goals to the good, courtesy of Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli.

A West Ham fan sings in the stands; Jake Cooper of Millwall and Morato of West Ham square off as their teammates try to separate them (below).

Mohamadou Kanté got West Ham back in the game in the 74th minute and six minutes later Konstantinos Mavropanos restored parity.

Afterwards there were a few brief scuffles between Millwall supporters and police outside the ground, but they quickly petered out. Within minutes, young fans were waiting by the stadium for autographs while others stood around discussing the match.

To an outsider, the similarities between Millwall and West Ham can appear greater than their differences. Many supporters I have met have friends or relatives on the other side, and both clubs draw heavily on values of working-class London such as toughness, loyalty and authenticity. Yet when they meet there remains real animosity among sections of both fanbases. Perhaps that is part of what gives the rivalry its intensity – both clubs are competing, in different ways, to represent a similar place, culture and identity, and to claim themselves as the more authentic expression of it.

Millwall and West Ham have now played one another across three centuries. The docks that gave the fixture its name have largely disappeared, the clubs have moved further apart and competitive meetings have become increasingly rare. But the competition over what each club represents, and the need to distinguish one side from the other, has survived.

West Ham supporters argue across the rail tracks with Millwall supporters on the road below.

articles.content:
The league phase kicks off this week, with several sides optimistic of unseating the European champions

T his competition is wide open. “But, wait, you say that every year!” No, honestly, this time it is wide open. The league phase of a new Women’s Champions League campaign begins on Tuesday with genuine elements of unpredictability, intrigue and a competitive feel after Barcelona, the holders, and winners of four titles in six years, underwent significant changes this summer.

The Spanish champions, who have reached six European finals in a row, have had four players who started the victory in the final last season leave the club . Ona Batlle joined Arsenal , Salma Paralluelo signed for OL Lyonnes – against whom she scored twice in that 4-0 victory to clinch the title in May – and Alexia Putellas and Mapi León moved to London City Lionesses. They have a very different look and feel to the formidable aura they demonstrated in Oslo.

They are still the team to beat, though, and retain an excellent squad, including the winner of the last three Ballons d’Or in Aitana Bonmatí – although she is doubtful for their opener against Paris FC on Wednesday with injury – as well as the top scorer in the competition last season, Ewa Pajor, and their captain, the Spain midfielder Patri Guijarro.

It will still take a world-class team to topple them, but there is perhaps no longer that same air of invincibility accompanying them this time.

Hoping to capitalise and reclaim a title they have not won since 2022 – a relatively long wait given they are the record eight-time winners – are OL Lyonnes. They had a comparatively good transfer window, adding Paralluelo, who scored her first goal for the club on Friday during an 8-1 demolition of Le Havre, and the Scotland midfielder Caroline Weir , who joined after four years at Real Madrid.

Lifting the European Cup would be a defining achievement for their owner, Michele Kang, who also owns Washington Spirit and London City Lionesses, and for their head coach, Jonatan Giráldez, if he could win the competition with a second team after his back-to-back successes with Barcelona in 2023 and 2024.

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: I awoke to the sound of my bedroom bin rustling

articles.content:
At first the mice were just a distant pitter-patter. But soon they had an unblinking confidence that they owned the entire house and all the food in it

L iving in a nine-person house in Vancouver, Canada, far from my UK home, came with plenty of benefits. Cleanliness was not one of them. A dish left behind quickly multiplied and bins overflowed in little more than a day. I’m not saying the endless strew of disposable coffee cups was the cause of our year-long mice infestation, but it no doubt helped.

In the winter of 2023, one of my housemates began to hear the sound of creatures rattling around in the ceiling of her basement room. The pitter-patters grew louder and louder; others began to report sightings from across the house. It wasn’t long before I was waking to the sound of my bedroom bin rustling. I had to accept it: we had mice.

When I saw my first mouse scuttling across the kitchen floor, my body filled with dread at the battle I knew we had ahead. Sleep quickly became a luxury. My housemate claimed she could hear hundreds of mice partying above her head. Frustrated with her inability to sleep, she would regularly hit her ceiling panels and be rewarded by a mouse falling on her face in return.

There was rarely a day when any food left in the cupboard hadn’t been gnawed through. I spent many mornings staring at my sourdough bread and questioning whether the large holes in it were from natural causes or mouse-made. I even began to believe I could recognise the taste of food that had also been sampled by our tiny friends. It all sounds mad, but it became hard to work out what was real or not when every time you walked into a room you were greeted by a squeal.

We tried to get rid of them. Exterminators came and left, to no avail. The steel wool we placed over any holes was easily chewed through. Nothing seemed to stop the furry creatures from infesting every part of our home. I told myself they’d be gone in the warmth of summer. But summer came, and the mice remained.

As time passed, they grew in confidence. I’d watch as they casually walked towards me while I sat at my desk. I’d shoo one away and it would barely move, staring back blankly as if I posed no threat. Eventually I just accepted their presence and resigned myself to the occupation of my space. The most brazen incursion came one morning when a housemate woke to find a mouse chewing their hair.

I don’t remember exactly when the infestation ended, or if I just left the house before the mice did, but I know I’ll never again dismiss the sight of one mouse. Behind one lies a hundred.

articles.content:
A long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and art

A t 69, I had never hiked with a backpack and I had no idea what land art was. Nonetheless, when my friend Jackie, a nature documentary film-maker, invited me to join her and her friends Wendy and Sasha on a hiking trip to Refuges d’Art in the mountainous countryside of Haute-Provence, I said a resounding “yes”. We would be sleeping alongside sculptures by the renowned land artist Andy Goldsworthy .

First, I watch Rivers and Tides , a documentary on Goldsworthy’s work, and discover he has built exquisite ice sculptures and stone cairns in my own country, Canada. His work seems to speak to an older part of the soul. Then, I start walking up hills, gradually adding weights to my backpack until I can comfortably carry 9kg (20lb).

We meet in Digne-les-Bains, a bustling mountain town in the centre of the Unesco geopark of Haute-Provence , and the starting point for a 10-day, 150km (93-mile) hiking route that includes the possibility of staying overnight at seven reservable but free off-grid sleeping cabins. Goldsworthy worked alongside local teams to restore the abandoned shepherd huts, farmhouses, chapel and stone shelters, and created a site-specific artwork for each one. Over four days, we will visit three of these refuges and hike about 45km (28 miles).

Our first stop in Digne-les-Bains is Maison Alexandra David-Neél , a museum dedicated to the adventurous, peripatetic life of a woman who, in 1924, disguised herself as a beggar to become the first western woman to enter the Forbidden City of Lhasa in Tibet. The keys to the refuges are kept here, no doubt, to inspire hikers for the adventures that lie ahead.

On the first day, we encounter one of three sentinels that sit like giant mysterious eggs watching over the route. These 2 to 3-metre tall cairns were made by Goldsworthy without mortar or cement and rely on fitting the right shapes and weights of the stones.

Jackie has told us the trail is mostly flat and indeed, we start on even gravel, chatting and laughing, getting used to the weight of our packs. After 5km, she says we should look for a path leading up the hill on our right. She checks her satnav and points to a goat path going straight up the rocks. I panic. My backpack suddenly feels extremely heavy. In desperation, I check further down the road and, to everyone’s relief, find a path marked with white and red horizontal lines signifying a grande randonnée , a trail certified by the French government.

We begin our ascent, pausing to photograph curlicued and wispy plants right out of Dr Seuss, yellow, scarlet and blue wildflowers, an orange moth sitting on purple brush. Spanish broom perfumes the air. We lift our gaze and see multiple valleys and unique geological formations. It’s easy to imagine our ice-age ancestors walking these trails 15,000 years ago and it’s gratifying to be travelling under our own steam, as they did.

We arrive at the first refuge, La Forest , as the sun is setting. The key unlocks the door. Inside, the air is cold. Our eyes adjust to the dark. A table and benches stand in front of us. To the left, a stairway leads to sleeping platforms. To the right, a doorway into a dark, empty room. From its depths glows a cylindrical obelisk, light falling on one large stone where someone could sit. It’s concave, constructed of light grey stone ending in a porthole to the sky. It’s illuminated by natural light and changes with the time, the weather, the season. This art is living and feels sacred.

That evening, we eat freeze-dried mushroom risotto in the flickering candlelight, play cards, eat chocolate, laugh and share stories. Sasha, who works in film in Germany, teaches us two words: der salzlose – someone who is bland and without flavour; and extrawurst – someone who always demands more. Neither apply to our group. The camaraderie and conviviality bring pure pleasure.

We climb the stairs to the sleeping platforms. Wendy and Sasha have brought sturdy sleeping mats on Jackie’s recommendation. We lay them out and say goodnight. The quiet is complete. Then, a tidal wave of sound erupts. Wendy and Sasha have rolled over. The friction on the technical fabric of their sleeping mats is deafening. The price of comfort has been revealed; they must lie like mummies.

The next day, we descend, picnic by a river on crackers, avocados and cheese, then start climbing again. Sasha and I subversively agree that it’s psychologically better to be told something is going to be hard and then it turns out easier. I console myself that climbing with a backpack is good for bone density and way less boring than lifting weights.

The next refuge, Le Vieil Esclangon , is in a mountain-top meadow. A majestic fan of lifted rock shines across the wide valley. Everywhere we turn there are more mountains and valleys. The first floor of the refuge is a large dark room split in two by a massive fireplace. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms look out on to a sunlit verge. Across from the fireplace, a tall serpentine shape made of dried mud loops back and forth like a meandering river, ending at the top in the source.

The wind picks up and the temperature drops. We gather wood and light a fire. In the flickering orange light, the sculpture comes to life, looking like one of Plato’s eternal forms. We eat our freeze-dried pad thai, the art and the hikers transient and temporary but together in this warm and cosy moment.

Later, we sleep to the sound of wind and rain, woken only by a mouse rave in the middle of the night.

We arrive at the third refuge, La Ferme Belon , in time for a late lunch. In the basement, huge interlinked semicircular stone arches look like a dragon’s body swimming through earth. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms are lovely except for one small detail. A colony of bats hang above. I can feign nonchalance because I know Wendy, who is quietly uber-capable, will find us a delightful B&B for the night. Over pizza and cold rosé, Sasha and I confess to Jackie that we would have rather known how challenging the hikes were going to be. “But you wouldn’t have come if I’d told you,” she answers with a twinkle in her eye.

Andy Goldsworthy said: “To me there is a tremendous difference between works of art that we observe in a museum just for a few minutes and works of art in which we live for a short while, in which we sleep. To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea.”

In Digne-les-Bains we return the keys and soak our stronger bodies in the town’s hot springs. We’ve already said yes to Jackie’s next adventure, sight unseen.

Claudia Casper’s novel The Mercy Journals won the Philip K Dick award for distinguished science fiction in 2017 (Arsenal Pulp Press)

articles.title: My son has left home – and I feel full of complicated joy | Zoe Williams
articles.summary: I took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your mother When kids are small, and their expectations of an event diverge from yours in some important way, you feel terrible about it. You might be taking them to a play, and they thought that meant they’d be allowed to play, but actually it meant they had to sit still while strangers shouted things. articles.content:
I took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your mother

W hen kids are small, and their expectations of an event diverge from yours in some important way, you feel terrible about it. You might be taking them to a play, and they thought that meant they’d be allowed to play, but actually it meant they had to sit still while strangers shouted things. You experience their disappointment as much as your own physical pain.

Then when they’re “adults”, your expectations diverge again. They thought you’d drop them at university and immediately leave, while you thought you’d unpack, and meet their flatmates, explore the city, and spin round a supermarket, then have a Nando’s, and maybe read a bedtime story, get chatting to the other parents and maybe all do karaoke? Well, then it’s time to manage your own disappointment, and the only thing to be said for that is that it’s way less bad than managing theirs.

When I went to university, my mum’s boyfriend drove me and there wasn’t room for her in the car, so it was a beautifully symmetrical event: I wanted him to leave and he wanted to leave. Then when she came to see me, I would count down the hours until she had to leave, and I used to love it when other people’s mums came to see them, because often they were nice, but, also, the schadenfreude was intense.

Mothers out of context are appalling. I don’t think there’s a feeling I’ve ever had that I remember with more clarity. Tugging on that memory unspooled the whole Technicolor exhilaration of suddenly having your own context, that your mother is absolutely not in. So there was more joy in being rejected by my son after dropping him off than you’d think, plus I went to KFC with his out-of-context dad on the way home and they gave us some free chicken selects. Don’t know why, maybe because we looked so complicatedly overjoyed.
