articles.title: Sumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipe
articles.summary: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken, onion and flatbread with tahini yoghurt, and a simple, textured salad Fattet musakhan , a celebration of two beloved Palestinian dishes, takes centre stage here, bringing together crisp bread, creamy yoghurt, sumac-spiced onions, tender chicken and fragrant olive oil in one rich and comforting dish. Alongside, the salad brings a welcome freshness, with crisp cucumber, creamy avocado and bright acidity cutting through the richness of the chicken. Together, they make a beautifully balanced meal, bringing the generous, communal spirit of Palestinian cooking to the table. Continue reading...
articles.content:
A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken, onion and flatbread with tahini yoghurt, and a simple, textured salad

Fattet musakhan , a celebration of two beloved Palestinian dishes, takes centre stage here, bringing together crisp bread, creamy yoghurt, sumac-spiced onions, tender chicken and fragrant olive oil in one rich and comforting dish. Alongside, the salad brings a welcome freshness, with crisp cucumber, creamy avocado and bright acidity cutting through the richness of the chicken. Together, they make a beautifully balanced meal, bringing the generous, communal spirit of Palestinian cooking to the table.

Fattet musakhan is a fusion of two dishes – sumac chicken, and crisp flatbread with tahini and yoghurt – brought together into one generous meal.

4 pitta (160g), cut into 5cm chunks 75ml olive oil , plus extra for serving Salt and black pepper 1½ tsp ground cumin 1½ tbsp sumac , plus extra for sprinkling ¼ tsp ground cinnamon ¼ tsp ground allspice 800g boneless skinless chicken thighs 2 tbsp lemon juice 30g pine nuts 1 large red onion , peeled and thinly sliced (250g net) 5g flat-leaf parsley , roughly chopped For the yoghurt sauce 400g greek-style yoghurt , to serve 40g tahini 1 garlic clove peeled and crushed 2 tsp lemon zest 2 tbsp lemon juice ¾ tsp salt

Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Put the pitta on a tray lined with greaseproof paper, add a tablespoon of olive oil and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt, and mix well. Spread the bread out in one even layer and roast for 10 minutes, turning once halfway, then remove and leave to cool. Turn up the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.

Put all the spices in a small bowl and mix well. Put the chicken in a large bowl with two tablespoons of oil, half the spice mix, the lemon juice, a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Mix well, then spread out on a second paper-lined baking tray. Roast for about 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Remove from the oven and set aside – keep any juices that have collected in the tray (pour these over the finished dish). When the chicken has cooled slightly, shred the meat into long strips and return to the tray.

Meanwhile, put the remaining two tablespoons of oil in a large saute pan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for two to three minutes, until golden. Transfer to a bowl lined with kitchen paper, leaving the oil in the pan.

Put the onion and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt in the hot oil left in the pan and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 15 minutes on a medium heat, until the onions are completely soft and pale golden (but not caramelised). Mix in the remaining spice mix and some black pepper, until the onions are completely coated.

To assemble the dish, arrange the pitta in one layer on a large platter or in a deep bowl. Spoon half the yoghurt sauce on top, scatter over half the chicken pieces, followed by half the onions. Repeat with the remaining yoghurt, chicken and onion, then pour all the tray juices around the bread. Garnish with the pine nuts, parsley, a good sprinkle of sumac and drizzle of olive oil.

Fresh, simple and wonderfully refreshing, this brings together avocado and cucumber for a lovely contrast of textures. The bright dressing adds freshness and acidity, making it the perfect accompaniment to rich dishes. I love salads like this, because they’re uncomplicated yet full of character.

3 ripe avocados (350g), peeled and stoned 3 tbsp lemon juice 300g cucumber (about 4-6 mini cucumbers or 1 large cucumber) 1 little gem lettuce , cut into large chunks 3-4 spring onions (70g), trimmed and thinly sliced 3 tbsp olive oil Red chilli flakes , or your favourite hot sauce, to serve (optional)

Cut the avocado flesh into 1cm cubes and put in a large bowl. Add the lemon juice and stir gently.

Peel the cucumber in alternating strips, then cut into bite-size pieces and put in the avocado bowl. Add the lettuce, spring onion, olive oil and a teaspoon of salt, then fold everything together until the avocado turns creamy and coats the salad, while most of the avocado remains in chunks.

Transfer the salad to a platter and finish with a sprinkle of chilli, if using.

articles.title: The truth about Sean Combs: ‘No is not a stopping point for him’
articles.summary: Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. articles.content:
Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-ins

F or Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, the civil lawsuit that dropped on Sean “Diddy” Combs in November 2023 seemed to come from nowhere. Filed by his ex-partner, the singer Cassie Ventura, it alleged that Combs had beaten and raped her, plied her with drugs and forced her into sexual encounters with male sex workers throughout their decade-long relationship.

Roundtree, along with much of the world’s media, was shocked. “I’d grown up in the era of Diddy and Cassie and viewed them as this power couple,” she says. “Her hit Me & U was my song. Diddy was this mogul – I knew him for the music – and she was this style inspiration, this beautiful, talented woman living an amazing life.”

At first, Combs and his legal team issued blanket denials. The lawsuit, they said, had followed an attempt by Ventura to blackmail Combs, and was “riddled with baseless and outrageous lies”. Despite this, they settled it immediately with a $20m sum, but within days more women came forward. A second lawsuit was filed one week after Ventura’s, by Joi Dickerson-Neal, which alleged that, as a student in 1991, she had been drugged and raped by Combs, who had filmed the alleged assault and shared it with other men. Days later came another. In this, Anna Kane alleged that Combs and two others had gang-raped her in 2003 when she was 17. As the cases piled up, Combs’s team continued the denials – describing the lawsuits as “money grabs”. Then a leaked video forced them to change tack. Security footage from a Los Angeles hotel taken in March 2016 showed Cassie Ventura creeping from a room, pursued by Combs, who is wrapped in just a towel. He beats her, kicks her and drags her back.

“His attorneys took it head on,” says Roundtree. “They were saying: ‘We’re going to own the domestic violence, but that happened in the past – all that is locked in the 2010s and he has changed. He has become Love since then. [Combs had declared in November 2017 that he was renaming himself Love, or Brother Love.] He’s a new person, a father figure.’ But all these other lawsuits were telling a completely different story.”

Roundtree started digging through the archives, finding stories, interviews and police reports lost to time, often because they weren’t online. Over the next three years, she spoke to people who had known Combs at every stage of his life – as a boy, a teenage intern, a genius producer and the founder of Bad Boy Records, a Grammy-winning artist, a business mogul – and finally as an inmate in a New Jersey prison. The lawsuits led to a federal investigation and, eventually, Combs’s indictment. Now 56, he is serving a 50-month sentence for transporting people across state lines for prostitution.

“To me, he was always ‘Diddy’,” says Roundtree. “When I talk to anyone from New York, he’s Puff or Puffy. Later, he wanted the world to call him Love and now, in this legal sense, he has become Sean Combs. He lives in these different versions for different people, but who is he?” Her book, Bad Boy for Life, attempts to answer this by picking out the patterns and repeat behaviours, the rumours and run-ins that have threaded through every reinvention. It reads like a “making of a monster”, a damning indictment of celebrity culture, where every impulse, however dark, is enabled by yes men. “I never planned to write a book but I was finding so much material, it felt important to preserve all the history in one place,” she says. “I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment.”

It begins in Harlem where Combs spent his first years, and where his father, a gangster, was shot dead when Combs was a toddler. His mother, Janice, moved them to Mount Vernon, a suburb of Westchester County, just north of New York City. The Janice remembered by Combs’s childhood friend Tim Patterson cuts a formidable figure – glamorous, determined and ambitious. Patterson describes discipline that goes beyond “tough love”, and wild parties where it was normal to walk in on couples “butt naked”.

“His childhood leaves questions that only Combs and Janice can answer,” says Roundtree, “but the sources from that time said that being exposed to sexual things quite young, parenting style and growing up in Harlem meant that, by the time he was a teenager at Howard University, you’re seeing that something had manifested.”

Janice Combs has complained of “lies” and “inaccuracies” in how she and her son’s upbringing have been portrayed.

At Howard, studying business, Combs was well known – for his drive, his style and his legendary parties. Years later, he also described falling in love at Howard, in an ill-fated Romeo and Juliet-style affair. In a magazine interview, Combs said his girlfriend’s parents disapproved because her grades had dropped from As to Bs. They pulled her from Howard, allowing her back only if she ended the relationship. “That hurt so bad. It’s one of those things in life that everybody goes through, but the pain was so intense it was hard for me to handle,” he said.

Former classmates remember it differently. In their accounts to Roundtree, Combs was jealous and abusive. His girlfriend’s parents intervened, they said, only after Combs had shown up at her dorm, called her outside, whipped her with his belt and dragged her by her hair, while students watched horrified from their windows.

“The way he romanticised all that, and talked about her as if they were destined by the stars but forces kept them apart, was exactly how his attorney talked about Cassie decades later,” says Roundtree. “In the trial last year, the attorney called Combs’s relationship with Cassie ‘a great modern love story’.”

The pages of Bad Boy for Life are packed with allegations, many involving women who have since launched civil suits. (Up to 70 lawsuits are believed to be moving through the system.) There are common features: one-night encounters where drinks are spiked, a woman is raped, and the alleged abuse is filmed, and others that tell how Combs would single out a woman and pursue her relentlessly using any means necessary. (“No is not a stopping point for Combs,” says Roundtree.) He was known for his untamed rage. Many former friends and colleagues describe witnessing his assaults on girlfriends – and on any men deemed rivals.

Roundtree also shines a light on other criminal activities in his orbit, from long-forgotten police reports to the notorious murders of his protege Biggie Smalls and Biggie’s rival, Tupac Shakur. Again, she picks out parallels. In 2001, after a shooting inside a Manhattan nightclub, Combs was charged with the possession of illegal weapons and attempted bribery (it was alleged that he had offered his driver $50,000 to take the blame). By then, at 31, Combs was already a multimillionaire with a record label, a fashion brand and a celebrity girlfriend, Jennifer Lopez. “His team conducted – and won – that early case in just the same way they fought the trial in 2025,” says Roundtree. “The smooth PR, the publicists who would talk to journalists and the crowds outside rooting for him.”

In that 2001 case, the jury acquitted Combs but his co-defendant, rapper Jamal “Shyne” Barrow, who had been with him on the night, was convicted, sentenced to 10 years, then deported to Belize, his birth country. Combs didn’t attend Barrow’s sentencing, quietly dropped Barrow from his record label and changed his name from Puff Daddy to P Diddy to mark his fresh start. (Barrow later described Combs as “someone who destroyed my life”.)

In every chapter of the book – and Combs’s life – people around him are shot, assaulted, imprisoned and broken, and careers are destroyed, yet he remains A-list, ascending to icon status. How? “That’s the biggest question,” says Roundtree. “How is someone with so many incidents around him, so much ruin in his wake, able to just keep doing better and better?

“I think part of it was his personality. The media loved him because he played into the spectacle – he wasn’t afraid to be larger than life. He was also building something people really believed in. His record company was everywhere in New York, and he was giving opportunities to young people, straight out of school. He’d created a living legend in Biggie, who died so early. His clothing line was cool. His fragrance was great. His parties were epic. All these things played into a figure so big and so tangible, people think they can see it all right in front of them. So why look any further?”

Ventura’s lawsuit was a pulling back of the curtain. “She was the first to let people into that world,” says Roundtree. “It’s really rare to see the inner workings of a public couple, but she laid it all out there, through her lawsuit, her trial testimony with all those photos on screen and text messages that she was asked to read, in front of the jury, in front of the world. She bared it all.”

Ventura had signed to Combs’s record label when she was 19, a model turned singer. She had a hit, Me & U, a 10-album deal, and so much promise ahead. The book describes Combs’s focused pursuit of her, despite the 17-year age gap. (One of his personal assistants recalls Combs describing her as “very mouldable” and saying: “I got her right where I want her. She’s young.”)

Combs’s inner circle and Ventura’s testimony describe the control he had over every part of her life – her diary, clothes, hair, nails. Even her medical records went directly to Combs’s email and he tracked her menstrual cycle. Her career stalled. Though Ventura recorded hundreds of tracks, her boss – Combs – didn’t release them. “She was his ‘wife partner’ for 10 years publicly,” says Roundtree. “One of the most surprising things to see was that, behind the scenes, she never lived with him, she never spent Christmas with him.”

The relationship described by Ventura was dominated by “freak-offs” – coerced, multi-day-long, drug-fuelled sexual encounters with male sex workers, held in hotel rooms. Every aspect was micromanaged, choreographed, directed, watched and filmed by Combs. According to Ventura, she was 22 when Combs first raised the idea, and she “had no concept of how it would be a turn-on”. But she wanted to please him. After the first, she felt “dirty” but glad Combs was “happy” with her, that she “did something right”.

Hundreds more took place around the world with unvetted men she didn’t know. Ventura says she felt “disgusting”, “humiliated”. When she attempted to leave Combs, he threatened to share the videos. (In one exchange between them, she talks of showing the world photos of her beaten face and body. “Release the videos also,” Combs shoots back.) Her life became preparing for “freak-offs”, enduring them and recovering afterwards. (“That’s why nothing gets done,” she wrote in one message to Combs, in 2017, their final year together. “Always healing.”)

Ventura officially separated from Combs in 2018 and filed her lawsuit five years later. When federal investigators subsequently approached her to build a criminal case, she handed over phones, iPads, video material, the names of sex workers and other witnesses to help corroborate her claims.

The US has no federal laws around coercive control and offences such as rape and assault carry statutes of limitations – legal time limits after which prosecution is not possible. But Combs was charged with racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution. “Those laws were developed to bring down the mafia, to dismantle criminal networks,” says Roundtree.

Combs’s 2025 trial lasted seven weeks, with the prosecution arguing that Combs used his business empire as a front for a criminal operation, relying on close associates to force and intimidate women into freak-offs and transport and supply drugs to keep them compliant. The defence argued successfully that what took place did not constitute a formal criminal enterprise. Ultimately, he was acquitted of most charges . “He was only found guilty of the clear examples where he paid for the male escorts to travel across a state line,” says Roundtree. “If they’d stayed within their states, they couldn’t have charged him with that.”

The music industry, says Roundtree, is yet to have its “#MeToo fallout”. “Hollywood had this reckoning; music never really has.” R Kelly is the only other high-profile musician now in prison because of abuse uncovered in the me-too fall out. Others have been untouched by swirling rumours and mounting accusations. “Maybe it’s because an artist is so singular,” says Roundtree. “Actors have this whole machine around them, procedures to go through, people to answer to. And we love our music. Those songs are our fondest memories, they take us right back to a place or a time or a person and it’s hard to give that up, to separate the art from the artist. Sean Combs was a producer. Do we give up every song he touched? So we can’t listen to Biggie any more? It’s not realistic.”

Combs’s release date is set for early in 2028, and he has multiple civil cases still to answer, although on Thursday it was reported that his attorneys are no longer acting for him in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills. What lies beyond this? “He’ll definitely want to try to tell his story and make a comeback,” says Roundtree. “He has had a microphone in his hand since he was in his early 20s and I don’t think that desire to be loved and validated has gone away. There’ll be a next chapter for Sean Combs.”

Bad Boy for Life: The Rise and Fall of Sean Combs by Cheyenne Roundtree (Simon & Schuster, £25) is out on 29 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

Despite this, they settled it immediately with a $20m sum, but within days more women came forward. A second lawsuit was filed one week after Ventura’s, by Joi Dickerson-Neal, which alleged that, as a student in 1991, she had been drugged and raped by Combs, who had filmed the alleged assault and shared it with other men. Days later came another. In this, Anna Kane alleged that Combs and two others had gang-raped her in 2003 when she was 17. As the cases piled up, Combs’s team continued the denials – describing the lawsuits as “money grabs”. Then a leaked video forced them to change tack. Security footage from a Los Angeles hotel taken in March 2016 showed Cassie Ventura creeping from a room, pursued by Combs, who is wrapped in just a towel. He beats her, kicks her and drags her back.

“His attorneys took it head on,” says Roundtree. “They were saying: ‘We’re going to own the domestic violence, but that happened in the past – all that is locked in the 2010s and he has changed. He has become Love since then. [Combs had declared in November 2017 that he was renaming himself Love, or Brother Love.] He’s a new person, a father figure.’ But all these other lawsuits were telling a completely different story.”

Roundtree started digging through the archives, finding stories, interviews and police reports lost to time, often because they weren’t online. Over the next three years, she spoke to people who had known Combs at every stage of his life – as a boy, a teenage intern, a genius producer and the founder of Bad Boy Records, a Grammy-winning artist, a business mogul – and finally as an inmate in a New Jersey prison. The lawsuits led to a federal investigation and, eventually, Combs’s indictment. Now 56, he is serving a 50-month sentence for transporting people across state lines for prostitution.

“To me, he was always ‘Diddy’,” says Roundtree. “When I talk to anyone from New York, he’s Puff or Puffy. Later, he wanted the world to call him Love and now, in this legal sense, he has become Sean Combs. He lives in these different versions for different people, but who is he?” Her book, Bad Boy for Life, attempts to answer this by picking out the patterns and repeat behaviours, the rumours and run-ins that have threaded through every reinvention. It reads like a “making of a monster”, a damning indictment of celebrity culture, where every impulse, however dark, is enabled by yes men. “I never planned to write a book but I was finding so much material, it felt important to preserve all the history in one place,” she says. “I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment.”

It begins in Harlem where Combs spent his first years, and where his father, a gangster, was shot dead when Combs was a toddler. His mother, Janice, moved them to Mount Vernon, a suburb of Westchester County, just north of New York City. The Janice remembered by Combs’s childhood friend Tim Patterson cuts a formidable figure – glamorous, determined and ambitious. Patterson describes discipline that goes beyond “tough love”, and wild parties where it was normal to walk in on couples “butt naked”.

“His childhood leaves questions that only Combs and Janice can answer,” says Roundtree, “but the sources from that time said that being exposed to sexual things quite young, parenting style and growing up in Harlem meant that, by the time he was a teenager at Howard University, you’re seeing that something had manifested.”
Janice Combs has complained of “lies” and “inaccuracies” in how she and her son’s upbringing have been portrayed.

At Howard, studying business, Combs was well known – for his drive, his style and his legendary parties. Years later, he also described falling in love at Howard, in an ill-fated Romeo and Juliet-style affair. In a magazine interview, Combs said his girlfriend’s parents disapproved because her grades had dropped from As to Bs. They pulled her from Howard, allowing her back only if she ended the relationship. “That hurt so bad. It’s one of those things in life that everybody goes through, but the pain was so intense it was hard for me to handle,” he said.

Former classmates remember it differently. In their accounts to Roundtree, Combs was jealous and abusive. His girlfriend’s parents intervened, they said, only after Combs had shown up at her dorm, called her outside, whipped her with his belt and dragged her by her hair, while students watched horrified from their windows.

“The way he romanticised all that, and talked about her as if they were destined by the stars but forces kept them apart, was exactly how his attorney talked about Cassie decades later,” says Roundtree. “In the trial last year, the attorney called Combs’s relationship with Cassie ‘a great modern love story’.”

The pages of Bad Boy for Life are packed with allegations, many involving women who have since launched civil suits. (Up to 70 lawsuits are believed to be moving through the system.) There are common features: one-night encounters where drinks are spiked, a woman is raped, and the alleged abuse is filmed, and others that tell how Combs would single out a woman and pursue her relentlessly using any means necessary. (“No is not a stopping point for Combs,” says Roundtree.) He was known for his untamed rage. Many former friends and colleagues describe witnessing his assaults on girlfriends – and on any men deemed rivals.

Roundtree also shines a light on other criminal activities in his orbit, from long-forgotten police reports to the notorious murders of his protege Biggie Smalls and Biggie’s rival, Tupac Shakur. Again, she picks out parallels. In 2001, after a shooting inside a Manhattan nightclub, Combs was charged with the possession of illegal weapons and attempted bribery (it was alleged that he had offered his driver $50,000 to take the blame). By then, at 31, Combs was already a multimillionaire with a record label, a fashion brand and a celebrity girlfriend, Jennifer Lopez. “His team conducted – and won – that early case in just the same way they fought the trial in 2025,” says Roundtree. “The smooth PR, the publicists who would talk to journalists and the crowds outside rooting for him.”

In that 2001 case, the jury acquitted Combs but his co-defendant, rapper Jamal “Shyne” Barrow, who had been with him on the night, was convicted, sentenced to 10 years, then deported to Belize, his birth country. Combs didn’t attend Barrow’s sentencing, quietly dropped Barrow from his record label and changed his name from Puff Daddy to P Diddy to mark his fresh start. (Barrow later described Combs as “someone who destroyed my life”.)

In every chapter of the book – and Combs’s life – people around him are shot, assaulted, imprisoned and broken, and careers are destroyed, yet he remains A-list, ascending to icon status. How? “That’s the biggest question,” says Roundtree. “How is someone with so many incidents around him, so much ruin in his wake, able to just keep doing better and better?

“I think part of it was his personality. The media loved him because he played into the spectacle – he wasn’t afraid to be larger than life. He was also building something people really believed in. His record company was everywhere in New York, and he was giving opportunities to young people, straight out of school. He’d created a living legend in Biggie, who died so early. His clothing line was cool. His fragrance was great. His parties were epic. All these things played into a figure so big and so tangible, people think they can see it all right in front of them. So why look any further?”

Ventura’s lawsuit was a pulling back of the curtain. “She was the first to let people into that world,” says Roundtree. “It’s really rare to see the inner workings of a public couple, but she laid it all out there, through her lawsuit, her trial testimony with all those photos on screen and text messages that she was asked to read, in front of the jury, in front of the world. She bared it all.”

Ventura had signed to Combs’s record label when she was 19, a model turned singer. She had a hit, Me & U, a 10-album deal, and so much promise ahead. The book describes Combs’s focused pursuit of her, despite the 17-year age gap. (One of his personal assistants recalls Combs describing her as “very mouldable” and saying: “I got her right where I want her. She’s young.”)

Combs’s inner circle and Ventura’s testimony describe the control he had over every part of her life – her diary, clothes, hair, nails. Even her medical records went directly to Combs’s email and he tracked her menstrual cycle. Her career stalled. Though Ventura recorded hundreds of tracks, her boss – Combs – didn’t release them. “She was his ‘wife partner’ for 10 years publicly,” says Roundtree. “One of the most surprising things to see was that, behind the scenes, she never lived with him, she never spent Christmas with him.”

The relationship described by Ventura was dominated by “freak-offs” – coerced, multi-day-long, drug-fuelled sexual encounters with male sex workers, held in hotel rooms. Every aspect was micromanaged, choreographed, directed, watched and filmed by Combs. According to Ventura, she was 22 when Combs first raised the idea, and she “had no concept of how it would be a turn-on”. But she wanted to please him. After the first, she felt “dirty” but glad Combs was “happy” with her, that she “did something right”.

Hundreds more took place around the world with unvetted men she didn’t know. Ventura says she felt “disgusting”, “humiliated”. When she attempted to leave Combs, he threatened to share the videos. (In one exchange between them, she talks of showing the world photos of her beaten face and body. “Release the videos also,” Combs shoots back.) Her life became preparing for “freak-offs”, enduring them and recovering afterwards. (“That’s why nothing gets done,” she wrote in one message to Combs, in 2017, their final year together. “Always healing.”)

Ventura officially separated from Combs in 2018 and filed her lawsuit five years later. When federal investigators subsequently approached her to build a criminal case, she handed over phones, iPads, video material, the names of sex workers and other witnesses to help corroborate her claims.

The US has no federal laws around coercive control and offences such as rape and assault carry statutes of limitations – legal time limits after which prosecution is not possible. But Combs was charged with racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution. “Those laws were developed to bring down the mafia, to dismantle criminal networks,” says Roundtree.

Combs’s 2025 trial lasted seven weeks, with the prosecution arguing that Combs used his business empire as a front for a criminal operation, relying on close associates to force and intimidate women into freak-offs and transport and supply drugs to keep them compliant. The defence argued successfully that what took place did not constitute a formal criminal enterprise. Ultimately, he was acquitted of most charges . “He was only found guilty of the clear examples where he paid for the male escorts to travel across a state line,” says Roundtree. “If they’d stayed within their states, they couldn’t have charged him with that.”

The music industry, says Roundtree, is yet to have its “#MeToo fallout”. “Hollywood had this reckoning; music never really has.” R Kelly is the only other high-profile musician now in prison because of abuse uncovered in the me-too fall out. Others have been untouched by swirling rumours and mounting accusations. “Maybe it’s because an artist is so singular,” says Roundtree. “Actors have this whole machine around them, procedures to go through, people to answer to. And we love our music. Those songs are our fondest memories, they take us right back to a place or a time or a person and it’s hard to give that up, to separate the art from the artist. Sean Combs was a producer. Do we give up every song he touched? So we can’t listen to Biggie any more? It’s not realistic.”

Combs’s release date is set for early in 2028, and he has multiple civil cases still to answer, although on Thursday it was reported that his attorneys are no longer acting for him in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills. What lies beyond this? “He’ll definitely want to try to tell his story and make a comeback,” says Roundtree. “He has had a microphone in his hand since he was in his early 20s and I don’t think that desire to be loved and validated has gone away. There’ll be a next chapter for Sean Combs.”

Bad Boy for Life: The Rise and Fall of Sean Combs by Cheyenne Roundtree (Simon & Schuster, £25) is out on 29 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

articles.content:
People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis

A December 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”. Progress indeed.

Nearly six decades on, electric toothbrushes can do a lot more than merely jiggle, offering multiple speeds and movement sensors for real-time tracking of where you’ve brushed – some even promise gum-massage or tongue-cleaning modes. Prices range from about £25 for a basic Oral B model to £599.99 for a Philips Sonicare model that gives “smart coverage feedback”. The latest super-toothbrush – a mere £419.99 – features a camera and a built-in water jet to clean between teeth, using AI to identify gaps. Created by Dyson, it’s still, essentially, a stick with a brush on the end (although there is another toothbrush on the market that’s shaped like a mouthguard, with individual brushes, that claims to clean your teeth in 20 seconds).

In the UK, 59% of adults use an electric toothbrush and sales, including replacement heads, reached £361m in the last year, according to market intelligence company Mintel. Any product launch by Dyson – still associated with reinventing the vacuum cleaner – feels like something of an event, so its incursion into oral health does feel significant, says Rachel Bairsto, the head of museum services at the British Dental Association. “We’re seeing more and more expensive toothbrushes,” she says. “Expensive toothpaste as well.”

These highly designed everyday objects have become symbols of affluence. “If you see a picture of a swanky bathroom, it will definitely have plug sockets for some kind of rechargeable electric toothbrush,” says Bairsto. “Whereas I’ve tried to look through the archives to find pictures of bathrooms with toothbrushes in them, and I can’t. Was everybody appalled at the sight of a toothbrush in the bathroom? I don’t know.” With many toothbrushes now, she says, “I think there’s definitely a status symbol [aspect] to it.”

We’re more interested in oral health than ever, says Dr Zaeem Jafri, a dentist and the founder of Nova Smiles, an online advice website. “From what I’ve seen from my patients, people are more conscious about it, wanting to avoid dental treatment, wanting their teeth to look nice and feel nice, and I think a lot of people are turning to gadgets to help.” Another dentist, Dr Reena Wadia, known as Dr Reena, a periodontist or gum specialist at the RW Perio clinic in London, says: “Gum health has become super topical. One reason why is because there’s really good evidence now that gum health is linked to your general health , so gum health is now part of the wellness conversation. People are taking it more seriously.” There is growing evidence that gum disease, she says, comes with an “increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Those are the two key ones, [but] there’s lots of other conditions related to it.” A poor oral microbiome has been associated with a range of diseases, including Alzheimer’s and several types of cancer, as well as depression.

Both Dr Reena and Jafri recommend rechargeable electric toothbrushes over manual ones, but neither are urging their patients to go out and buy a Dyson brush, or spend similar sums on other brands. “There’s no robust research that says a certain kind of electric brush removes plaque at a better rate than others,” says Jafri.

Jafri has tested Dyson’s CameraJet, along with many other electric toothbrushes. He found it messy – the water jet was hard to angle, and he says it didn’t seem to find all the gaps between his teeth. He points out that a non-foaming toothpaste is needed for an adequate camera view – sold by Dyson, with the cheapest at £8.49. The live stream to a phone app was a novelty, but in reality he says it was hard to see much with water, teeth and the inside of his cheeks in the way. Cameras in toothbrushes, says Jafri, “have the potential to be good. If patients had cameras that were detecting chipped and broken fillings and can send those images to a dentist to review [and] spot things early, that would be a phenomenal advancement. For Dyson right now, it’s using the camera to detect when the brush is in the right position to shoot the water jet – it didn’t really work that well for me. It’s a bit of an overkill.”

Another concern is that the water jet rinses away the toothpaste when most dentists now recommend spitting, not rinsing, so the fluoride in it stays on and around the teeth for longer. Dr Reena adds: “[The water jet may] make people think, oh, I don’t need to floss, or I don’t need to use interdental brushes. But actually, that jet is an adjunct, not a replacement.” Niamh Turney, a Dyson engineer who worked on the CameraJet, says, however, “The goal is to make interdental cleaning easier and more convenient for those who aren’t already managing to fit flossing into their routine.”

There have been reports of some brushes overheating, and charging problems; at the time of writing, the brush was unavailable to buy. Dyson says it is aware that “a small number of early batches may have experienced a component issue. We are isolating those batches and are taking all the necessary steps to support our customers,” and that there are “some shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production. We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an oral health crisis . It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children are more than three times more likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.

The first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch and Boots , alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.

Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”

It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”

As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”

One of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”

Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”

Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.

“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”

We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an oral health crisis . It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children are more than three times more likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.

The first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch and Boots , alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.

Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”

It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”

As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”

One of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”

Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”

Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.

“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”

articles.title: Celia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing show

One is Britain’s grandest luxury name, the other the textile designer who dressed bohemian 1960s London in her prints and has a place in art history as David Hockney’s favourite muse. Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closed London fashion week was born. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection

Burberry and Celia Birtwell are both national treasures of sorts. One is Britain’s grandest luxury name, the other the textile designer who dressed bohemian 1960s London in her prints and has a place in art history as David Hockney’s favourite muse.

Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closed London fashion week was born.

Burberry’s calling card is a graphic check; Birtwell is all blowsy doodled florals and psychedelic snaking vines. “The check is so dominant and so brilliant that at first I thought: what can I do here?” Birtwell said before the show. She hand-painted a less regimented version, which Lee loved. “She made the check more human. If you are buying a luxury product it’s not a necessity, it’s an emotional purchase, so it needs to feel human.” A doodle of round, Smartie-bright faces from her archive, drawn 20 years ago but never produced, became another print of the season.

The mood of the show, held around the corner from Burberry HQ at Chelsea School of Art, was buoyant: charming prints, soft silhouettes, and the eclectic guest list that is as much a Burberry signature as the check itself: actor Fiona Shaw and footballer Djed Spence on the front row, with rapper Central Cee making a cameo on the catwalk.

Burberry is bouncing back from its crisis years , steered by its chief executive, Joshua Schulman , and designer Lee. This summer, the brand reported its first revenue growth in three years, as retail sales rose 5% year-on-year in the second quarter. Schulman’s strategy is offering “value for money in a luxury context”, which translates as pivoting from an ill-fated attempt to sell Burberry handbags at Hermès prices to more realistic price tags. Lee has brought a youthful, gen Z inflection to the Britishness that is Burberry’s calling card.

A successful element of its turnaround has been Burberry zeroing in on the outerwear market, where Burberry has bona fides to best every other name. British heritage is a trump card when it comes to coats, and the appeal of the Burberry name reaches from arctic explorers to football fans. For this summer collection, trenches came in slinky silk taffeta, with puffball hems and ruched collars; one model carried an embroidered umbrella, against summer showers.

To amplify its London fashion week message, Burberry is staging a small display in an upstairs gallery of the V&A museum in South Kensington, which will be open to the public until 3 January. The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon includes a military overcoat worn by a lieutenant colonel in the British army in 1939, designer Hardy Amies’ own Burberry trench, as well as metallic leather and gold snakeskin runway trenches from recent catwalk shows.

articles.title: The best plastic-free cutting boards: I spent six weeks testing 10 boards, and these won

It’s a must-have for any recipe that needs chopping, smashing, mincing, carving or sometimes even serving. And, let’s be honest, it’s also where we pile up other kitchen items while we make a mess. articles.content:
A good, sturdy chopping board will last you many years. I tested the best non-plastic, non-toxic ones, including some made out of wood and synthetic rubber

A cutting board is literally the foundation of most things you cook. It’s a must-have for any recipe that needs chopping, smashing, mincing, carving or sometimes even serving. And, let’s be honest, it’s also where we pile up other kitchen items while we make a mess.

Plastic cutting boards are affordable and convenient, but research shows they shed significant amounts of microplastics into food. And though the health damage caused by microplastics is still being studied , we don’t need microplastics in our minestrone.

Many people believe that plastic cutting boards are more hygienic, but a study from the Journal of Consumer Protection and Food Safety found only minor differences “in microbiological counts” on wooden and plastic chopping boards “after proper cleaning” ( how to clean a cutting board ). Plastic boards also tend to get scratched up more than their natural alternatives.

To help you avoid plastics, I tested a bunch of non-toxic, plastic-free cutting boards in my home. Good chopping boards should be sturdy, gentle on kitchen knives, easy to clean and versatile. My picks are below.

Be sure to check out our guides to the best plastic-free kitchen upgrades , best non-toxic pans and how to clean a cutting board .

This guide has been updated for fall 2026. We made a bunch of tweaks to help you navigate easier, added some advice and accessories, sharpened our wording and added a section to explain what we do here at The Filter. We will continue to update it as we test.

“Boos Blocks” are some of the best-loved cutting boards out there; my maple R-Board has been a reliable workhorse in my kitchen for almost nine years. This cheaper model has curved corners for easy handling, and comes in a variety of sizes, from 10in x 10in to 20in x 15in, meaning it can fit both your budget and your counter space.

For $60, this wood cutting board is sturdy, well-constructed and easy to use. I also loved the rounded edges, which made it easy to handle – it would double beautifully as a grazing board. Once I gave it a few coatings of board oil, it became much more resistant to stains, too. ( John Boos also sells board cream and oil , or you can get your own. It helps seal the wood and protect it from warping or splitting.)

There are a variety of sizes to choose from when selecting a board, which I liked. I went with a bigger model, but the difference between a 16in and 18in board can be crucial in a smaller kitchen. Many of the heftier, more expensive options only had one or two sizes.

It’s a shame that … since this is an edge-grain board, the texture of the wood is a little rougher and requires some additional TLC from board oil or cream to help seal it.

Material Kitchen has been making a recycled plastic cutting board for years. The brand has finally come up with a plant-based plastic (a “bioplastic”) that doesn’t shed permanent microplastics (it does shed, but they break down over time). It’s technically a plastic, but made from biological substances rather than petroleum, and it offers the same ease, affordability and lightness without the microplastics.

I found myself whipping out this board any time I needed to handle raw meat. It’s light, so pulling it out from its storage spot between two shelving units for a quick job felt just as easy as grabbing a spatula; washing it was a breeze.

It’s slim, but has a small juice groove that held exactly the amount of liquid expressed from a whole, raw chicken while I stuffed and trussed it for roasting. (I still placed a tea towel beneath in case of spills.) It didn’t pick up any smells, and I really loved the color options: I picked a gentle ocean blue, but you can also go for a “shell” pink or off-white. It’s dishwasher-safe too.

It’s a shame that … this cutting board did start showing knife marks pretty quickly. This is standard for a plastic board, but I still don’t love how the marks look.

Brooklyn Butcher Blocks sources all its wood from within the US, and the company designs its boards with the aim to minimize waste, composting “ even the smallest remnants ”. For me, the company’s sustainable practices are a happy bonus: if I’m trying to eliminate plastic from my kitchen, I also want to eliminate waste from my kitchen tools’ production.

This is an expensive beautiful cutting board. The dark walnut is elegant and damn near sultry. The brickwork pattern shows off the board’s sturdy “end grain” nature.

The board didn’t retain any knife marks and cleaned easily. Some people claim that walnut retains more smells than cherry or maple, since the grain is slightly more open. However, across my testing I didn’t have any issue with transferring smells – as long as I washed my board after each use.

I found this 16in board to be the perfect size for my small kitchen: hefty enough to handle my prep needs, but not so large that it felt cumbersome to wash.

It’s a shame that … like all good wooden cutting boards, it requires hand-washing, which can feel daunting. It’s also nearly $500, which is far, far above most reasonable cutting board budgets. Still, I love it.

The Asahi board is made with synthetic rubber, which offers a gentle give that hard plastic doesn’t have. Rubber cutting boards are a favorite of sushi chefs, who use them to slice raw fish with incredibly sharp knives. And if sushi chefs around the world trust a rubber board to preserve the sharpness of their blades, so do I.

The Asahi’s surface was as firm and comforting as a new mattress. (It was a stark contrast to the titanium board I tested, which made my knife feel like it was slipping around on a freshly Zamboni-smoothened ice rink.) Synthetic rubber is especially easy on knives, and its weight means that it won’t slip around on your countertop. Since the material is non-porous, it’s also antibacterial.

While it’s not dishwasher-safe, this cutting board was especially easy to clean in the sink, and it doesn’t require the oiling and waxing that wooden boards do. Also, unlike the Material Kitchen board in this guide, it didn’t show knife marks.

It’s a shame that … of all my picks, this board held onto smells the most. Make sure to give it a really thorough wash after every use – or only use it to prep savory dishes. And again, it is not dishwasher safe.

Like the Brooklyn Butcher Block, this is a large and sturdy end-grain cutting board that can take pride of place on your countertop. I loved how dramatically tall this board is: the board itself is 2in thick, and it stands on taller-than-average rubber feet. I’m on the tall side (5ft 9in), and my prep space isn’t particularly high, so I liked how this board brought my prep work a few inches higher.

Its maple wood did hold some stains, but I thought the brickwork pattern was particularly beautiful.

It’s a shame that … when it comes to big-ticket, end-grain cutting boards, my preference is walnut thanks to its good looks and ability to hide stains. ( This board also comes in walnut for $50 more .)

I also find it a little annoying to wash boards that have rubber feet. But if you like the height and sturdiness of this model, it’s a stunning option for your countertop.

Etsy seller The Pinocchio Workshop makes beautiful end-grain boards out of Milford, Connecticut. This board had beautiful walnut wood that hid stains and dazzled the eye, with a striking, two-toned brickwork pattern. It almost looked like a more elegant version of one of those magic eye posters.

Like the other butcher blocks here, you can customize your board – by size, or by adding finger grooves, a juice groove or rubber feet for stability. I went for the 10in x 15in board, which is perfect for prepping a solo dinner or setting out a grazing board for a small party. They also offer custom engraving, making it an ideal gift.

It’s a shame that … it isn’t a slightly thicker board, but this is mostly a question of preference. At 1.5in, it is thicker than many boards I tested and the thickness is not a true negative.

For wooden boards that aren’t suited for the harsh, battering cycle of a dishwasher, hand-washing is necessary. And while it can feel laborious, the best way to take care of your wooden cutting boards is to wash them after each use. If that feels like a gargantuan task, you should wash them at least once a week. That way, odorous gunk and bacteria doesn’t get a chance to build up too much.

Start by wiping them down with a cloth or rag soaked in hot water to help remove any gunk or debris. Then use mild dish soap and a non-abrasive sponge to clean the board all over – that means, bottom, edges and corners too! (I love the compostable Blueland sponges .) Dry it well. And if you’re gonna store it anywhere but your countertop, store it vertically – this can help prevent warping.

To increase your board’s longevity, invest in food-safe mineral oil and some sort of board wax or “butter”. Once a month or so, add a drizzle of oil to your cutting board before rubbing it in with a soft, clean cloth. Don’t go too crazy with the oil; you want just enough to coat.

Leave the board standing on its edge to dry and absorb the oil overnight; the next day, seal it with a food-grade wax, ideally one designed for cutting boards.

Use a soft cloth (like microfiber) to really spread it over the wood, though again, don’t go overboard in your application. After another 12 hours or so to let the wax absorb, you can buff off any excess with a cloth.

It may sound like a lot of work, but a well-maintained wooden board lasts years, and that payoff is worth investing in.

For more tips on maintenance and care, read: How to properly clean your cutting board .

Our mission is to help you filter out junk products and buy fewer, better things.

At the Filter US , we test the products we recommend ourselves and never take your trust for granted. We also consider possible impacts on your health or the environment in our coverage and companies cannot purchase a spot in our product rankings because we are here to serve you, not corporations.

Our team is a part of the Guardian’s US editorial team and our journalists follow its strict ethical standards. Learn more about us here .

I’ve been writing about food for over a decade, whether that’s writing cookbooks, reviewing restaurants for the New York Times or testing recipes for publications such as Food52 and chefs including April Bloomfield.

I’m an obsessive home cook with a small kitchen: my cutting boards not only serve as chopping blocks, but also storage spaces, tea trays and serving platters. I use mine at least a few times a day, whether I’m chopping vegetables for lunch, breaking down a chicken for dinner or just containing the mess of my tea setup.

I selected 10 of the top plastic-free cutting boards to test: six wood cutting boards and four wood alternatives, including rubber and stainless steel. For the wood boards, I chose both edge-grain and end-grain wood boards, which have different benefits. (More on that later.) I didn’t test any glass cutting boards because their hard surfaces can very quickly dull or chip your knives.

I tested the boards for six weeks in my own kitchen, where I started by getting to know them: turning them around in my hands, moving them between different spots in my kitchen, and giving them a good out-of-the-box clean. A great cutting board should be something you can handle easily. Even if you want a big honking slab of wood that will spend most of its time looking pretty on your countertop, you still need to clean it in the sink. I kept asking myself: does this board feel hefty? Puny? Can I store it easily, or will it take pride of place on my (admittedly very small) countertop?

Then I got to chopping. This is what we do on cutting boards. We chop, we slice, we smash, we mince, we move little piles of stuff around until we’re ready to add it to a pan or pot. And if you’ve ever used a flimsy cutting board on a granite countertop, you know how things can go awry. (Pro tip: fold a tea towel and place it underneath the board to keep it from slipping.)

I chopped a bunch of onions on each board to see how smooth that felt.

I also designed a Sniff Test to measure whether or not a board held onto oniony, garlicky smells: I chopped at least one very large onion on each board, washed it well with unscented dish soap, then gave it a big, officious sniff.

I alternated between Material Kitchen’s 8in knife and a Japanese knife I got as a gift about a decade ago.

And I donated the cutting boards I tested to St Mary’s Clothing Drive, a wonderful charity near my apartment in Brooklyn.

Finding the right board means asking yourself a few questions. Do you just want a beautiful board that you can use to display spreads of meat and cheeses – with the occasional chopping of an onion? Do you cook yourself elaborate meals every night? Are you looking for the cheapest option?

A sustainable bioplastic board: Boards like the Material Free Board will give you the lightness, ease and price point of a traditional plastic board without shedding microplastics into your lunch.

Butcher block-style wooden boards: These are easily customizable, which is nice. Consider their different sizes, or adding finger grooves, rubber feet or a juice groove.

End grain cutting boards: These are the hardiest wooden boards you can buy – and the easiest on your knives. They are made by taking small pieces of hardwood and gluing them together vertically. When the grain tracks vertically, rather than horizontally, the wood can self-heal, even after lots of chopping. These boards do require more maintenance; you really want to invest in that oil and wax. You cannot put these in a dishwasher.

Edge grain cutting boards: In these, the grain is running horizontally across your cutting board. These boards are still much easier on your knives than plastic (or, god forbid, glass), but they can show wear and knife marks more easily. They are also more affordable.

Caraway review: I tested the nonstick and nontoxic cookware – the good, bad and cheaper alternatives

Marian Bull is a freelance writer with over 10 years of experience in writing and testing recipes, chopping endless onions and hand-washing her cutting board in her tiny kitchen. Her favorite food is fried toast.
