Once I gave it a few coatings of board oil, it became much more resistant to stains, too. ( John Boos also sells board cream and oil , or you can get your own. It helps seal the wood and protect it from warping or splitting.)

There are a variety of sizes to choose from when selecting a board, which I liked. I went with a bigger model, but the difference between a 16in and 18in board can be crucial in a smaller kitchen. Many of the heftier, more expensive options only had one or two sizes.
It’s a shame that … since this is an edge-grain board, the texture of the wood is a little rougher and requires some additional TLC from board oil or cream to help seal it.

Material Kitchen has been making a recycled plastic cutting board for years. The brand has finally come up with a plant-based plastic (a “bioplastic”) that doesn’t shed permanent microplastics (it does shed, but they break down over time). It’s technically a plastic, but made from biological substances rather than petroleum, and it offers the same ease, affordability and lightness without the microplastics.

I found myself whipping out this board any time I needed to handle raw meat. It’s light, so pulling it out from its storage spot between two shelving units for a quick job felt just as easy as grabbing a spatula; washing it was a breeze.

It’s slim, but has a small juice groove that held exactly the amount of liquid expressed from a whole, raw chicken while I stuffed and trussed it for roasting. (I still placed a tea towel beneath in case of spills.) It didn’t pick up any smells, and I really loved the color options: I picked a gentle ocean blue, but you can also go for a “shell” pink or off-white. It’s dishwasher-safe too.
It’s a shame that … this cutting board did start showing knife marks pretty quickly. This is standard for a plastic board, but I still don’t love how the marks look.

Brooklyn Butcher Blocks sources all its wood from within the US, and the company designs its boards with the aim to minimize waste, composting “ even the smallest remnants ”. For me, the company’s sustainable practices are a happy bonus: if I’m trying to eliminate plastic from my kitchen, I also want to eliminate waste from my kitchen tools’ production.
This is an expensive beautiful cutting board. The dark walnut is elegant and damn near sultry. The brickwork pattern shows off the board’s sturdy “end grain” nature.

The board didn’t retain any knife marks and cleaned easily. Some people claim that walnut retains more smells than cherry or maple, since the grain is slightly more open. However, across my testing I didn’t have any issue with transferring smells – as long as I washed my board after each use.
I found this 16in board to be the perfect size for my small kitchen: hefty enough to handle my prep needs, but not so large that it felt cumbersome to wash.

It’s a shame that … like all good wooden cutting boards, it requires hand-washing, which can feel daunting. It’s also nearly $500, which is far, far above most reasonable cutting board budgets. Still, I love it.

The Asahi board is made with synthetic rubber, which offers a gentle give that hard plastic doesn’t have. Rubber cutting boards are a favorite of sushi chefs, who use them to slice raw fish with incredibly sharp knives. And if sushi chefs around the world trust a rubber board to preserve the sharpness of their blades, so do I.

The Asahi’s surface was as firm and comforting as a new mattress. (It was a stark contrast to the titanium board I tested, which made my knife feel like it was slipping around on a freshly Zamboni-smoothened ice rink.) Synthetic rubber is especially easy on knives, and its weight means that it won’t slip around on your countertop. Since the material is non-porous, it’s also antibacterial.

While it’s not dishwasher-safe, this cutting board was especially easy to clean in the sink, and it doesn’t require the oiling and waxing that wooden boards do. Also, unlike the Material Kitchen board in this guide, it didn’t show knife marks.

It’s a shame that … of all my picks, this board held onto smells the most. Make sure to give it a really thorough wash after every use – or only use it to prep savory dishes. And again, it is not dishwasher safe.

Like the Brooklyn Butcher Block, this is a large and sturdy end-grain cutting board that can take pride of place on your countertop. I loved how dramatically tall this board is: the board itself is 2in thick, and it stands on taller-than-average rubber feet. I’m on the tall side (5ft 9in), and my prep space isn’t particularly high, so I liked how this board brought my prep work a few inches higher.
Its maple wood did hold some stains, but I thought the brickwork pattern was particularly beautiful.

It’s a shame that … when it comes to big-ticket, end-grain cutting boards, my preference is walnut thanks to its good looks and ability to hide stains. ( This board also comes in walnut for $50 more .)
I also find it a little annoying to wash boards that have rubber feet. But if you like the height and sturdiness of this model, it’s a stunning option for your countertop.

Etsy seller The Pinocchio Workshop makes beautiful end-grain boards out of Milford, Connecticut. This board had beautiful walnut wood that hid stains and dazzled the eye, with a striking, two-toned brickwork pattern. It almost looked like a more elegant version of one of those magic eye posters.

Like the other butcher blocks here, you can customize your board – by size, or by adding finger grooves, a juice groove or rubber feet for stability. I went for the 10in x 15in board, which is perfect for prepping a solo dinner or setting out a grazing board for a small party. They also offer custom engraving, making it an ideal gift.
It’s a shame that … it isn’t a slightly thicker board, but this is mostly a question of preference. At 1.5in, it is thicker than many boards I tested and the thickness is not a true negative.

For wooden boards that aren’t suited for the harsh, battering cycle of a dishwasher, hand-washing is necessary. And while it can feel laborious, the best way to take care of your wooden cutting boards is to wash them after each use. If that feels like a gargantuan task, you should wash them at least once a week. That way, odorous gunk and bacteria doesn’t get a chance to build up too much.

Start by wiping them down with a cloth or rag soaked in hot water to help remove any gunk or debris. Then use mild dish soap and a non-abrasive sponge to clean the board all over – that means, bottom, edges and corners too! (I love the compostable Blueland sponges .) Dry it well. And if you’re gonna store it anywhere but your countertop, store it vertically – this can help prevent warping.

To increase your board’s longevity, invest in food-safe mineral oil and some sort of board wax or “butter”. Once a month or so, add a drizzle of oil to your cutting board before rubbing it in with a soft, clean cloth. Don’t go too crazy with the oil; you want just enough to coat.
Leave the board standing on its edge to dry and absorb the oil overnight; the next day, seal it with a food-grade wax, ideally one designed for cutting boards.

Use a soft cloth (like microfiber) to really spread it over the wood, though again, don’t go overboard in your application. After another 12 hours or so to let the wax absorb, you can buff off any excess with a cloth.
It may sound like a lot of work, but a well-maintained wooden board lasts years, and that payoff is worth investing in.
For more tips on maintenance and care, read: How to properly clean your cutting board .
Our mission is to help you filter out junk products and buy fewer, better things.

At the Filter US , we test the products we recommend ourselves and never take your trust for granted. We also consider possible impacts on your health or the environment in our coverage and companies cannot purchase a spot in our product rankings because we are here to serve you, not corporations.
Our team is a part of the Guardian’s US editorial team and our journalists follow its strict ethical standards. Learn more about us here .

I’ve been writing about food for over a decade, whether that’s writing cookbooks, reviewing restaurants for the New York Times or testing recipes for publications such as Food52 and chefs including April Bloomfield.

I’m an obsessive home cook with a small kitchen: my cutting boards not only serve as chopping blocks, but also storage spaces, tea trays and serving platters. I use mine at least a few times a day, whether I’m chopping vegetables for lunch, breaking down a chicken for dinner or just containing the mess of my tea setup.

I selected 10 of the top plastic-free cutting boards to test: six wood cutting boards and four wood alternatives, including rubber and stainless steel. For the wood boards, I chose both edge-grain and end-grain wood boards, which have different benefits. (More on that later.) I didn’t test any glass cutting boards because their hard surfaces can very quickly dull or chip your knives.

I tested the boards for six weeks in my own kitchen, where I started by getting to know them: turning them around in my hands, moving them between different spots in my kitchen, and giving them a good out-of-the-box clean. A great cutting board should be something you can handle easily. Even if you want a big honking slab of wood that will spend most of its time looking pretty on your countertop, you still need to clean it in the sink. I kept asking myself: does this board feel hefty? Puny? Can I store it easily, or will it take pride of place on my (admittedly very small) countertop?

Then I got to chopping. This is what we do on cutting boards. We chop, we slice, we smash, we mince, we move little piles of stuff around until we’re ready to add it to a pan or pot. And if you’ve ever used a flimsy cutting board on a granite countertop, you know how things can go awry. (Pro tip: fold a tea towel and place it underneath the board to keep it from slipping.)
I chopped a bunch of onions on each board to see how smooth that felt.

I also designed a Sniff Test to measure whether or not a board held onto oniony, garlicky smells: I chopped at least one very large onion on each board, washed it well with unscented dish soap, then gave it a big, officious sniff.
I alternated between Material Kitchen’s 8in knife and a Japanese knife I got as a gift about a decade ago.
And I donated the cutting boards I tested to St Mary’s Clothing Drive, a wonderful charity near my apartment in Brooklyn.

Finding the right board means asking yourself a few questions. Do you just want a beautiful board that you can use to display spreads of meat and cheeses – with the occasional chopping of an onion? Do you cook yourself elaborate meals every night? Are you looking for the cheapest option?
A sustainable bioplastic board: Boards like the Material Free Board will give you the lightness, ease and price point of a traditional plastic board without shedding microplastics into your lunch.
Butcher block-style wooden boards: These are easily customizable, which is nice. Consider their different sizes, or adding finger grooves, rubber feet or a juice groove.

End grain cutting boards: These are the hardiest wooden boards you can buy – and the easiest on your knives. They are made by taking small pieces of hardwood and gluing them together vertically. When the grain tracks vertically, rather than horizontally, the wood can self-heal, even after lots of chopping. These boards do require more maintenance; you really want to invest in that oil and wax. You cannot put these in a dishwasher.

Edge grain cutting boards: In these, the grain is running horizontally across your cutting board. These boards are still much easier on your knives than plastic (or, god forbid, glass), but they can show wear and knife marks more easily. They are also more affordable.

Marian Bull is a freelance writer with over 10 years of experience in writing and testing recipes, chopping endless onions and hand-washing her cutting board in her tiny kitchen. Her favorite food is fried toast.

articles.title: Victoria Starmer models clothes at London fashion week show
articles.summary: Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus Victoria Starmer has taken part in a London fashion week show, in one of her first public appearances since her husband, Keir Starmer, stepped down as prime minister. Lady Starmer appeared at Sunday’s Edeline Lee show. articles.content:
Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus

Victoria Starmer has taken part in a London fashion week show, in one of her first public appearances since her husband, Keir Starmer, stepped down as prime minister.

Lady Starmer appeared at Sunday’s Edeline Lee show. The London-based, Canadian British designer’s clothes are a favourite of the Princess of Wales, and have also been worn by celebrities including singer Taylor Swift and actor and screenwriter Phoebe Waller-Bridge.

Lee’s spring/summer 2027 show took place in the unusual setting of a north London school sports hall. Starmer wore a bright turquoise knitted midi dress with a high neckline, pleated detailing and short, sculptural sleeves, paired with white block-heeled shoes, with her hair worn in loose waves.

Rather than preparations for the show taking place backstage in the usual way, in Lee’s unique show, models were fitted and adjusted in full view of the audience, dancers rehearsed beside the catwalk, while a drone followed proceedings from the high ceiling of the gymnasium.

Starmer was photographed having her makeup done beside the catwalk, against a backdrop of a football net, with makeup and hair products spread out over a table in front of her. Ballerinas stretched beside the catwalk and synchronised swimming-inspired dancers performed in bright red costumes as part of the show, in the school in Chalk Farm.

The collection was based on the Greek myth of Sisyphus, in which a man is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down again each time he reaches the top.

“There’s a general feeling right now of relentlessness, a sisyphean cycle,” Lee said. “I was already thinking about the ballet – dance is incredibly transporting, but the work behind it is so intense, the way dancers train for years, the endless repetition, for one ecstatic moment of performance, and then they’re back in the studio.

“I wanted to acknowledge the rigour and hard work behind that moment – much like the skill and artistry required of my team to present beautiful clothes.”

Throughout Keir Starmer’s time in office, Lady Starmer kept a low public profile, but her “political chic” and “modern British” sense of style was often admired. She has favoured contemporary British brands, including ME+EM, Needle & Thread, and Edeline Lee, whose main creative design studio is based in east London.

At London fashion week’s spring/summer shows in 2024, when her husband was prime minister, Lady Starmer took a front-row seat at Edeline Lee’s show, which took place at Millbank Tower, a former campaign HQ of Labour and the Conservatives, where Reform UK’s central office is now based.

She wore a borrowed £615 cream pussy-bow blouse with a navy polka dot print and matching £715 wide-leg trousers.

It came amid a row over free clothes for Lady Starmer, with Keir Starmer facing an investigation at the time over a possible breach of parliamentary rules around gifts.

He had failed to declare that some of his wife’s designer clothes had been bought for her by his biggest personal donor, Lord Alli. The Sunday Times reported that the Labour peer had paid for a personal shopper, clothes and alterations before and after Starmer became prime minister.

articles.title: ‘I feel betrayed’: inside Ed Sheeran’s controversial return to the stage
articles.summary: Some fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of Palestine “This is not usually how I would open the show,” Ed Sheeran told the crowd at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night, a humble preamble to a three-plus-minute speech addressing the greatest controversy of his career. articles.content:
Some fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of Palestine

“T his is not usually how I would open the show,” Ed Sheeran told the crowd at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night, a humble preamble to a three-plus-minute speech addressing the greatest controversy of his career. Shaky-voiced and stealing glances at the monitor at his feet, he looked every bit the chastened superstar.

“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division, about humanity, not politics, but this is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it any more,” Sheeran said. He described the Hamas-led attack at the Nova music festival in Israel on 7 October 2023 as “horrific”, and expressed heartbreak over civilian deaths in Gaza and the West Bank, describing the situation as “catastrophic and unjustified and disproportionate”.

“Everyone here can stand by people that they don’t agree with on everything, but they can always agree on singing these songs,” he declared shortly before launching into Castle on the Hill, a rousing anthem about growing up in rural England. The guitar jangled, fireworks lit into the sky and pastoral scenes filled a giant screen behind the pop star as fans sang along. There was an overwhelming sense, between Sheeran and his ecstatic audience, of wanting to turn the page.

Cindy Lucente, a 73-year-old retiree who attended the show with her daughter and granddaughter, described the speech as “eloquent” and said that she was impressed by Sheeran’s mettle.

“People kept telling me I should probably get rid of my ticket because he’s going to cancel,” she said. “But I knew he wouldn’t.”

The night marked Sheeran’s return to the stage after the rapper Macklemore was removed from the tour after controversy erupted over his remarks during a performance at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 5 September. In a statement shared to Instagram last Tuesday, Sheeran said that he faced pressure from venue owners – including Robert Kraft , the billionaire who owns Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots – to excise Macklemore from the lineup, but that his removal “was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine”. The statement was met with widespread condemnation, with detractors accusing Sheeran of bowing to corporate interests and putting profit over freedom of expression.

“I feel betrayed about how he handled this,” said Hillary Steinberg, a 34-year-old sociology PhD who was among the pro-Palestine protesters gathered outside the NRG metro station, a group that reached about 100 at one stage. “It has sort of soured how I think about him as an artist.”

After getting her ticket refunded earlier in the week, Steinberg decided to come to the stadium and try convincing others to do the same. She wore a black and white keffiyeh and held a sign that read: “If you leave now you will have more spine than Ed Sheeran .” By the end of the night, she said that she and her boyfriend had convinced “at least five” other people to get refunds.

Despite reported safety concerns and fears of an outright cancellation, the mood at Lincoln Financial Field was light and at times triumphant. The singer repeatedly invoked the controversy but spoke in broad terms and with an air of self-deprecation. He did not mention Kraft or Macklemore by name.

“I hope you enjoyed the opening acts – I heard they were great,” Sheeran joked early in the show, waving off concerns about having to carry the event alone. Per its moniker, the Loop tour mostly features Sheeran performing solo and utilizing a looping pedal to create his own soundscapes.

One of the night’s many standing ovations came after Sheeran brought out a group of musicians, led by the fiddler Alicia Enstrom, to back him on a number of songs including the lilting Galway Girl. The Irish folk band Beoga, which had played behind Sheeran during this section on earlier stops, was among the acts who dropped out in solidarity with Macklemore. They were joined by the Danish band Lukas Graham, the Irish singer Aaron Rowe, and Finneas – brother and collaborator to Billie Eilish and a musician in his own right – who was slated to join Sheeran for a South American leg later this year.

Sheeran made it clear that Enstrom and the others were to be Beoga’s replacement.

“They said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought that I was a certain type of person,” Sheeran said to rapturous cheers from the audience.

Melody Fillier, a 49-year-old who works in the pharmaceuticals industry, was among those who applauded the new backing band.

The other conspicuous change was the absence of a retractable bridge and smaller “B-stage”, which had positioned the singer much closer to the crowd during intimate sections of earlier shows. Sheeran explained that he didn’t want to risk having things thrown at him.

“I took the B-stage out because I was afraid what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that,” he said, grinning sheepishly.

Throughout the night, Sheeran returned again and again to themes of political harmony. The pop star appeared less defiant than humbled, repeatedly describing the concert as the greatest of his career. It seems unlikely that his words, which mostly served to justify the actions of the preceding week, will satisfy his critics. But in the city of brotherly love, where the stadium appeared mostly full even as the concert stretched past the three-hour mark, fans of the singer seemed more than satisfied.

“I didn’t come here for politics,” said Tim Matkosky, a 59-year-old entrepreneur who was among those who stayed to the bitter end, up on their feet and dancing as the bassline thumped and fire plumes filled the air. “I came here to get away from politics.”

“I took the B-stage out because I was afraid what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that,” he said, grinning sheepishly.

Throughout the night, Sheeran returned again and again to themes of political harmony. The pop star appeared less defiant than humbled, repeatedly describing the concert as the greatest of his career. It seems unlikely that his words, which mostly served to justify the actions of the preceding week, will satisfy his critics. But in the city of brotherly love, where the stadium appeared mostly full even as the concert stretched past the three-hour mark, fans of the singer seemed more than satisfied.

“I didn’t come here for politics,” said Tim Matkosky, a 59-year-old entrepreneur who was among those who stayed to the bitter end, up on their feet and dancing as the bassline thumped and fire plumes filled the air. “I came here to get away from politics.”

articles.content:
This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes

Schmarr n , or schmarren , Anja Dunk writes, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation, pancake , a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and a batter pudding . Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports in her book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings , it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)

Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, including kaiserschmarren (studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.

All the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important. Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipe in The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who sent his recipe to the New York Times in 1980 in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.

My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes from Dunk and the Discover SüdTirol website , which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft and Hinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book , for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.

As Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.

Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargen kirschwasser , all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.

Both Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.

Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).

Traditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).

Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.

A cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). We also like Dunk’s crunchy flaked almonds, but both are entirely optional. As with the nutmeg, chopped hazelnuts, pecans or walnuts would make a fine substitute for those not concerned with authenticity, and even those who are should know that this can be served with any sort of fruit compote, and is particularly good with plums.

40g butter 90g flour ½ tsp salt 3 eggs 75ml milk 75ml cream (single, whipping or double), or 50ml extra milk Finely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemon (optional) 1 tbsp caster sugar 1 dessert apple 25g raisins , or currants or sultanas (optional) 1 tbsp icing sugar ½ tsp ground cinnamon (optional) Flaked almonds , to finish (optional)

Melt the butter in a medium ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat, leave to brown to a pale golden colour, then take off the heat – reheating will continue the browning process. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.

Put the flour and salt in a large bowl. Separate the eggs, then put the whites in a large glass or metal bowl and the yolks in a smaller bowl.

Beat the milk and cream, if using, into the egg yolks, then whisk into the flour to make a smooth batter. Stir in the lemon zest.

Beat the egg whites until foamy, then add the caster sugar and whisk to soft, creamy peaks that hold their shape but flop over at the top. Fold a little of the egg-white mix into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest.

Cut the apple into thin wedges, and remove and discard the core. Pour two tablespoons of the melted butter into a bowl, put the pan back on a medium heat and, once sizzling, pour in the batter. Arrange the apple slices and raisins, if using, on top, then leave to cook to a rich golden brown underneath. Carefully flip over the pancake (don’t worry if it breaks), then put in the hot oven for five minutes.

Meanwhile, mix the icing sugar with the cinnamon, if using. Use two forks to break the pancake into bite-size pieces. Tip out on to a plate or work surface and put the pan back on a medium-high heat with the reserved melted butter. Add the almonds, if using, and lightly toast, then top with the pieces of pancake and sprinkle with most of the sugar. Toss over the heat to coat, then divide between plates. Sprinkle with the remaining sugar and serve hot.

Schmarren, schmarrn – however you spell it, please share your wisdom on this homely Germanic mountain favourite. Or do you prefer to enjoy it in the sophisticated coffee houses of Vienna? Sweet or savoury? Fruity or plain? Baked or fried? All tips appreciated!

articles.content:
Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?

W hen I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side.

Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now …

As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else?

Thankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. Perhaps because I’d started with Orient Express, a glamorous setting was a foundational part of the Christie experience for me, especially after I’d watched the 70s film with Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman and Sean Connery sweeping down the platform trailing smoke and old-school Hollywood style. Poirot gets most of the fun, far-flung locations: the French Riviera, Egypt, the Greek islands and the Dolomites, to name a few.

To a younger reader, Miss Marple’s world initially felt quite small in comparison. It was only when I reread the books as an adult that I understood the genius of the character, and came to appreciate how clever and radical Christie had been in making an elderly spinster her master sleuth – occupying a space somewhere between that of a detective and a bystander. She had taken one of the “left behind” women – a figure typically both pitied and scorned by society for not having been able to find a partner after the first world war – and shown her running rings around the other characters, using her invisibility as a kind of superpower. And in creating Miss Marple, she had broken one of the oaths made by the Detection Club (of which Christie was a member) not to use “Feminine Intuition” as a means of solving the crime. So much in the Miss Marple books relies on her intuition: there are physical clues, yes, but it is her understanding of human nature, an understanding that is coded as specifically and peculiarly “female”, that really wins the day.

I came to appreciate Miss Marple’s lack of ego, her sense of humour: she is always in on the joke, always understands and plays up to the image others have of her. I enjoyed her sudden and surprising touches of darkness. I also loved that, while the Poirot books can feel quite timeless, the Marple books form a fascinating portrait of social change in Britain across the decades: the evolving landscape of the English village as documented between the 1930s setting of The Murder at the Vicarage and the 1950s period of The Mirror Crack’d from Side to Side (in which a new housing estate has been built), the postwar unease about not knowing one’s neighbours in A Murder Is Announced and the swinging 60s raciness of At Bertram’s Hotel.

All of which I came to appreciate anew when planning my own novel. I knew that Miss Marple herself was the key to it all, the element I had to get absolutely right. She had to be Christie’s Miss Marple in all her complexity and brilliance. The other vital factor was the perfection of Christie’s plotting: the element that had kept me up into the small hours as a preteen, trying to use all the tools provided to guess whodunnit.

But in other areas I knew that I had to break new ground. I didn’t want this book to be an exercise in ventriloquism – there was only one Agatha Christie, and to try to ape her exactly would be an exercise doomed to failure. It also wouldn’t be any fun, creatively. From the outset I realised that this would be a book in conversation with the original books, and indeed with other Agatha Christie books, but one that delivers new elements, and in doing so has its own raison d’être.

When I learned in my research that Death on the Nile was originally meant to be a Miss Marple novel, I found my jumping-off point: here was my way into the project. A way of including my own love of cinematic locations, and indeed what I had loved about those glamorous Poirot novels, in a new Miss Marple adventure. I would take her on holiday – high in the Swiss Alps, to the Grand Alpine Hotel, with its glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes. I realised, too, that using multiple first-person point-of-view narrators would be a fun way of replicating something Christie does so beautifully: telling us a great deal about her characters by showing how they react to Marple, how they by turns underestimate, admire or fear her.

Finally, I wanted my book to be in conversation with our own times. This wasn’t about shoe-horning in themes, but drawing out parallels between then and now. In doing so I wanted to interrogate modern society’s fear of ageing and the invisibility of old age that has hardly changed since Christie’s time. I wanted to highlight the prevalence of certain toxic male egos at the heart of culture and politics: figures who have attempted, at times, to rewrite history to further their own ends or disappear past misdeeds. All, apparently, with a total lack of consequence.

Which brings me to another thing I love about Christie’s writing: the grim satisfaction of seeing the past catching up with the wicked. The meting out of just deserts. It may not be happening out there in the real world at the moment, but rest assured, it happens here.

W hen I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side.

Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now …

As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else?

Thankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. Perhaps because I’d started with Orient Express, a glamorous setting was a foundational part of the Christie experience for me, especially after I’d watched the 70s film with Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman and Sean Connery sweeping down the platform trailing smoke and old-school Hollywood style. Poirot gets most of the fun, far-flung locations: the French Riviera, Egypt, the Greek islands and the Dolomites, to name a few.

To a younger reader, Miss Marple’s world initially felt quite small in comparison. It was only when I reread the books as an adult that I understood the genius of the character, and came to appreciate how clever and radical Christie had been in making an elderly spinster her master sleuth – occupying a space somewhere between that of a detective and a bystander. She had taken one of the “left behind” women – a figure typically both pitied and scorned by society for not having been able to find a partner after the first world war – and shown her running rings around the other characters, using her invisibility as a kind of superpower. And in creating Miss Marple, she had broken one of the oaths made by the Detection Club (of which Christie was a member) not to use “Feminine Intuition” as a means of solving the crime. So much in the Miss Marple books relies on her intuition: there are physical clues, yes, but it is her understanding of human nature, an understanding that is coded as specifically and peculiarly “female”, that really wins the day.

I came to appreciate Miss Marple’s lack of ego, her sense of humour: she is always in on the joke, always understands and plays up to the image others have of her. I enjoyed her sudden and surprising touches of darkness. I also loved that, while the Poirot books can feel quite timeless, the Marple books form a fascinating portrait of social change in Britain across the decades: the evolving landscape of the English village as documented between the 1930s setting of The Murder at the Vicarage and the 1950s period of The Mirror Crack’d from Side to Side (in which a new housing estate has been built), the postwar unease about not knowing one’s neighbours in A Murder Is Announced and the swinging 60s raciness of At Bertram’s Hotel.

All of which I came to appreciate anew when planning my own novel. I knew that Miss Marple herself was the key to it all, the element I had to get absolutely right. She had to be Christie’s Miss Marple in all her complexity and brilliance. The other vital factor was the perfection of Christie’s plotting: the element that had kept me up into the small hours as a preteen, trying to use all the tools provided to guess whodunnit.

But in other areas I knew that I had to break new ground. I didn’t want this book to be an exercise in ventriloquism – there was only one Agatha Christie, and to try to ape her exactly would be an exercise doomed to failure. It also wouldn’t be any fun, creatively. From the outset I realised that this would be a book in conversation with the original books, and indeed with other Agatha Christie books, but one that delivers new elements, and in doing so has its own raison d’être.

When I learned in my research that Death on the Nile was originally meant to be a Miss Marple novel, I found my jumping-off point: here was my way into the project. A way of including my own love of cinematic locations, and indeed what I had loved about those glamorous Poirot novels, in a new Miss Marple adventure. I would take her on holiday – high in the Swiss Alps, to the Grand Alpine Hotel, with its glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes. I realised, too, that using multiple first-person point-of-view narrators would be a fun way of replicating something Christie does so beautifully: telling us a great deal about her characters by showing how they react to Marple, how they by turns underestimate, admire or fear her.

Finally, I wanted my book to be in conversation with our own times. This wasn’t about shoe-horning in themes, but drawing out parallels between then and now. In doing so I wanted to interrogate modern society’s fear of ageing and the invisibility of old age that has hardly changed since Christie’s time. I wanted to highlight the prevalence of certain toxic male egos at the heart of culture and politics: figures who have attempted, at times, to rewrite history to further their own ends or disappear past misdeeds. All, apparently, with a total lack of consequence.

Which brings me to another thing I love about Christie’s writing: the grim satisfaction of seeing the past catching up with the wicked. The meting out of just deserts. It may not be happening out there in the real world at the moment, but rest assured, it happens here.

articles.title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario

articles.content:
Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China .

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay .

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.
Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.
“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

articles.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.summary: The comments were made at a summit in Ayrshire with participants from AI giants including Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
articles.content:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".

"No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."

Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".
